This study analyzes the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for calculating the ground state of a $d$-dimensional hypercube governed by the Schrödinger equation. A specific type of neural network, featuring $m$-component inputs and output constraints, is used to obtain an approximation of the ground state. The study reveals that for networks of size $N$ and a specific level of regularization, the generalization error for the ground state energy is minimized when the network size exceeds the cubic dimension of the cube, i.e., $N > O(d^3)$. Furthermore, under certain conditions, the approximate generalization error for the ground state is proportional to $N^{-1}$ multiplied by a term that increases polynomially with $d$, specifically $N \gg (d \log N)/\alpha$, where $\alpha$ represents the level of regularization. The findings follow from a non-asymptotic analysis of the Schrödinger equation's eigenvalues and eigenvectors on the $d$-dimensional cube with edge length $\sqrt{N}$. The analysis shows that the eigenvalues increase exponentially with $d$, the eigenvectors exhibit an Gaussian-like structure, and the distance between adjacent eigenvalues is of order $N$ divided by the volume of the cube. The findings suggest that for networks of size $N$ and a specific level of regularization, the ground state approximation is within an approximately $N$-dependent error margin, and this approximation is likely to be the best achievable with two-layer neural networks for solving this particular problem. The study also proposes an algorithm based on these findings, using networks of successive sizes to iteratively improve the approximation of the ground state. The results of this algorithm match the theoretical generalization performance, and upon examination, the ground states produced by these neural networks exhibited properties similar to those of the true ground states, such as exhibiting non-trivial symmetry-dependent variations when the network size exceeded a certain threshold. In surgical pathology, the assessment of tumor lymphocyte infiltration is crucial and essential for predicting various diseases' outcomes, including cancer. To develop a reliable and efficient method for quantifying this infiltration, we trained a neural network using a federation of institutional databases, each contributing histological images along with corresponding diagnoses. Due to the presence of diverse staining techniques across institutions, we employed semantic segmentation to accommodate various image modalities. Moreover, to mitigate balancing data and enhance generalizability, we utilized augmentation techniques. Following successful training, our model demonstrated exceptional balanced error rates on four distinct testing sets, achieving a sum of 7.47. Additionally, in a simulation of leaving one testing set uncontacted, our model maintained a strong performance, demonstrating minimal decline. Consequently, we believe this federated approach has great potential for collaborative training on diverse institutional collections, ultimately facilitating the deployment of models in real-world clinical settings. We have made our source code and training data framework available for public use through a GitHub repository at https://github.com/alexbosch/tqhtil. This study introduces a unified approach to quadrupedal movement control based on reinforcement learning in conjunction with an evolutionary algorithm. By utilizing an already-evolved pathway solution, the agent can learn its associated control parameters through reinforcement learning. The results demonstrate that this hybrid method enables the acquisition of pre-trained pathway models, which can then be integrated with reinforcement learning to train quadrupedal gaits. The evolutionarily-derived pathways serve as a prior knowledge, assisting the learning process and preventing undesirable movements such as "camping" (where one leg remains stationary while the other three move in a circular motion). Furthermore, this hybrid method facilitates multi-task learning capable of adapting to diverse objectives without the need for pre-defined safety constraints. The study showcases its effectiveness using realistic simulations of a four-legged robot. The underlying code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/Arjun-P-IndianInstituteOfTechnology/EPG. Severe suppression of X-ray emission has been observed in some AGNs, but the underlying cause remains unclear.  We present high-resolution Chandra data for the NGC 7213 galaxy, showing that its low-brightness AGN has a higher temperature than previously thought.  By using the high-resolution grating data, we found that the temperature is around 0.65 keV, which is supported by both the Si XIII and Si XIV lines.  This temperature agrees with those from other AGNs at similar luminosities.  We also found that the emission from iron around 6.4 keV is not of purely narrow-line emission, but is also supported by a broader component, likely originating from a higher temperature plasma.  Calculations indicate that the wind's plasma has a lower density and higher speed than typical in radio mode AGNs.  Data suggests that AGNs only exhibit tight correlations between radio power and X-ray spectral properties at high levels of radio power.  This research suggests that closed accretion discs and wind-launched jets are responsible for the radio power and X-ray spectral characteristics observed in high-brightness AGNs.  In contrast, low-brightness AGNs may be the result of other processes, such as a hot breeze, which we have evidence for in NGC 7213, or low collision rates within a hot gas, such as in photoionized plasmas.  Further investigation is needed to resolve conflicting theories and to determine the universal applicability of the 'radio mode' picture.  This research is a step towards understanding how AGNs lose energy through their surroundings, with potential links to the 'quenching' of AGNs through external energy absorption.  A more in-depth understanding of this will be crucial in understanding AGN evolution and its implications for galaxy evolution.  It is also possible that AGNs with low-brightness are actually in a state of transition, such as during changes in black hole mass or spin.  This could be further confirmed by observing AGNs with low-brightness that are also high in hard X-rays, such as through the use of NICER, which would indicate the presence of a nearby high-temperature plasma.  It is also possible to further understand AGN 'quenches' by observing nearby galaxies with low-brightness AGNs, such as through the use of e-ROSITA, which would allow for a study of low-brightness AGNs in a large sample of nearby galaxies. This research focuses on resolving a complex problem at its core, which stems from slight deviations in a critical system parameter, \psi. For the time being, \psi is maintained at a reliable value. Ultimately, we aim to find an innovative approach to rectify this issue through a model-free solution. Specifically, we tackle this challenge by first developing a straightforward algorithm to address a critical problem in a theoretical framework. Subsequently, we apply this model-free algorithm to a practical scenario, which involves a nonlinear system governed by a continuous dynamic equation. Lastly, we successfully combine this approach with an existing model-based concept, referred to as two-phase reinforcement learning, to develop a novel model-free reconfiguration system. Through our model-free reconfiguration, we are able to swiftly adjust and adapt \psi to optimize the performance of a given system in a realistic setting. As expected, our model-free reconfiguration exhibits faster response times and higher levels of performance compared to a traditional model-based approach. Notably, this model-free reconfiguration showcases robust results even in the presence of random disturbances, while a model-based reconfiguration may only function optimally under controlled conditions. Our success here marks a significant breakthrough in using model-free reconfiguration to replace model-based reconfiguration in practical, real-world applications. Additionally, our research paves the way for further innovation in the continuous reconfiguration of model-free systems. Essential code for this research is made available at https://github.com/AIUEABUE/Two-phase-reinforcement-learning. Additionally, relevant simulation data can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.6086/M2E3-J37K-9M1A-0C30-7UE2-5E3F-7T2E-4E3F. Finally, a detailed video demonstrating our model-free reconfiguration has been shared at https://doi.org/10.6086/M2E3-3A14-0C00-0C30-7UE2-5E3F-7T2E-4E3F. In 2010, the SiD Sensor collaboration submitted a proposal for a particle detector system designed for the future ILC, featuring an integrated luminescent gas chamber with photomultiplier sensors. Although the original concept demonstrated innovative problem-solving, significant modifications are required through integration with the BigWheel beam delivery system and active luminosity targeting. This will be achieved by replacing the original concept of a single large vessel with multiple smaller ones, equipped with optical fibers that enable the exchange of ions between compartments to counteract charge collection issues. Additionally, the detector design incorporates a novel umbrella design for electron collection, allowing for independent movement of electric field strength and position to optimize detection. Furthermore, optical sensors are replaced with highly sensitive low-power flat panel SiD sensors to streamline readout systems and reduce power consumption. This revised design addresses initial concerns regarding detection efficiency, charge collection, and particle identification, showcasing significant progress towards a final detector concept submission. Significant contributors to this revision include research on flat panel SiD sensors, charge collection strategies, and interactions within photomultiplier detectors, ultimately facilitating successful detector concept presentations to the ILC community in 2012 and 2013. Essential to these presentations were comprehensive R&D outcomes on detector components, charge collection, and luminosity targeting, as well as a thorough investigation of potential detector designs in the context of the ILC. This revised detector concept features an innovative modular design with luminescent gas chambers, optical sensors, and electric field configurations to optimize detection and charge collection, marking a major advancement towards a final submission for the ILC detector concept. Key to this concept are the technical capabilities and scientific outcomes from the SiD Sensor Collaboration's activities between 2010 and 2013. Furthermore, the proposal successfully addressed concerns and questions from the ILC community, as well as presentations and contributions to the detector conceptual work for the ILC. This led to a public submission of the detector concept for the ILC in 2014. In parallel to this concept development, the SiD Sensor collaboration continued demonstrating its commitment to work on a future ILC detector through various activities, including a series of extensive and comprehensive presentations on detector concepts, charge collection strategies, luminosity targeting, and innovative detector designs. This entailed contributions to the Annual ILC Community Workshop presentations in 2009, 2010, 2008-2013, and publications in Refs [1-4], as well as demonstrations of significant and varied R&D activities within the SiD Sensor collaboration, including contributions to the Annual ILC

A non-Newtonian fluid in which the heat of order arises from randomly moving components is known as an active nematic. It's characterized by two distinct time scales - one for the random movements and one for the fluid's flow. When the ratio of these time scales is significant, conventional fluid dynamics techniques struggle to provide accurate predictions. Our research uses the renormalization group formalism to explore this issue, focusing on how the fluid's properties change as its flow rate increases. We find that beyond a certain threshold, the fluid's order begins to decline, a phenomenon not supported by a simplified model based on a specific mathematical approach. Furthermore, the renormalization group formalism allows us to investigate the role of linear instability in a more complex model. It's worth noting that while both the simplified and complex models share some similarities with another type of complex fluid, the liquid crystal, their behavior differs significantly from each other. If it's driven by random movements, the simplified model applies, whereas the complex model is more accurate if it's driven externally. We examine the vector shape factor of the pion using a kaon bag model, taking into account the presence of glue in the bag. Our results for the vector shape factor show significant differences compared to existing calculations. Furthermore, incorporating the contribution of the pion vector shape factor into the hadronic vacuum polarization in the muon $(g-2)$ reveals a notable effect, amounting to 5\% of the total hadronic contribution. Our final estimate for the pion contribution to the hadronic vacuum polarization in the muon $(g-2)$ is $[5.15 \pm 2.15 (\mathrm{ex}.)_{\mathrm{QED})}] \times 10^{-9}$. Additionally, we compute the pion contribution to the hadronic electromagnetic and strong intermediate attractions in the muon $(g-2)$. Our findings suggest that these factors account for approximately 3\% and 2\% of the total hadronic contribution to the muon $(g-2)$, respectively. Our work also addresses ongoing discussions regarding the pion Gounaris-Sakurai parameter in the context of QCD. Our results indicate that the pion contribution to the hadronic electromagnetic and strong intermediate attractions in the low-energy pion regime can be described by the Gounaris-Sakurai parameter, provided that higher-order corrections and the effects of $K\bar{K}$ resonance are taken into account. A long-standing mystery in astronomy involves the relationship between a galaxy's mass and the mass of its central black hole. Over the past decade, research has consistently demonstrated that more massive galaxies tend to have larger black holes. However, the nature of this connection is not yet fully understood. To gain more insight, researchers used data from the ATLAS$^{\rm 3D}$ and SAMI galaxies to study how the black hole mass changes over time. They focused specifically on how this change relates to a galaxy's star formation history. Using advanced imaging techniques, they determined that more massive galaxies are able to sustain black hole growth for longer. Furthermore, they discovered that the rate at which black hole mass increases is higher during periods of star formation in the galaxy. This new finding provides significant evidence that a galaxy's mass and its black hole mass are connected through a shared physical process. As a result, the research suggests that a galaxy's early star formation history plays a key role in the development of its central black hole. The full study is available at arxiv.org/abs/2207.14164. The SAMI galaxy data used in the research can be accessed through the Catalogue of Galaxy Data, cataloguetools.github.io, and the ATLAS$^{\rm 3D}$ galaxy data through www.picoct.com/\~cortijo/atlas3d. The code for analyzing the data is available at github.com/ccarrillo05/BlackHoleEvolution. The research was conducted using computational resources provided by University of Sydney and University of Melbourne. The study's findings are based on a comprehensive dataset of 22,111 galaxies from the ATLAS$^{\rm 3D}$ and SAMI surveys, with a total of 198 galaxies which met the necessary criteria. By utilizing a sophisticated fitting process, researchers were able to determine black hole and halo mass for each galaxy. The resulting data revealed a significant and complex relationship underpinning black hole and halo development. The research indicates that a galaxy's early star formation history has a profound impact on both its black hole and halo mass, with more massive galaxies able to sustain black hole growth for longer. When comparing early and late star formation rates, the data revealed distinct patterns, with a notable result showing that black hole mass increases at the same rate regardless of a galaxy's final mass. This key discovery underscores the importance of a galaxy's early star formation history in black hole and halo development and provides a potential unified framework for understanding various scaling laws observed in galaxies. A specific approach, using pair measurements of dim and bright stars, is explored in more detail as it correlates with total aerosol optical depth. We present GGLasso, a Python package designed to address Generalized Graphical Lasso (GGL) problems. Building upon the Graphical Lasso (GL) framework, GGL introduces diverse real-valued matrix families whose positive Euclidean matrix completion leads to consistent Estimation of Confounding Variables in high-dimensional settings. At its core, GGLasso utilizes an iterative First Order Method and an active-subspace strategy to solve the GGL problem, also providing a Python interface for GL computation. Comprehensive documentation, including theoretical underpinnings and algorithmic motivations, as well as extensive numerical experimentation, complements the library. Furthermore, GGLasso incorporates a range of performance enhancements, including early termination based on smoothed objectives and premature termination of inactive variables. Numerical results demonstrate the efficacy of GGLasso, with a notable achievement being its capability to solve large-scale problems involving 270,000 variables in just a few minutes. With its versatility, GGLasso can handle various GGL problem formulations like Sparsity, Group Sparsity, and Graphical Lasso with a Neighborhood (GGLAN). Additionally, GGLasso facilitates the computation of an optimal graph, whose importance is substantiated by numerical experiments. Developed under the BSD license, GGLasso is freely accessible at https://gglasso.math.ucla.edu/. A comprehensive online supplement can be found at https://dx.doi.org/10.62421/gglasso.v1.0.1.

In this study, we utilise photoevaporation theory to explain the gluon emission observed in TW Hydrae through analysis of its spectral radio emission. We investigate how photoevaporation and magnetic forces impact the planet-forming disk around a 1 million year old, 0.12 solar masses star at a 2 astronomical units distance. According to the models, gas escaping from the disk should primarily be found within the innermost 10 astronomical units and ascending above the disk plane, with both photoevaporation and magnetic phenomena contributing to the observed gluon emission. We determine that the disk's mass loss rate due to photoevaporation ranges from 0.00010 to 0.00050 solar masses per year, and that magnetic forces significantly reduce the mass loss rate compared to purely photoevaporation processes. We use these results to make predictions for the observation of the CGS32 protostar in the nearby galaxy Caldwell 67 by utilizing ALMA towards the direction of CGS32, and we consider the potential for similar processes to affect the formation of exoplanets. Based on our analysis, we estimate that the overall mass loss rate due to photoevaporation in the planet-forming region of TW Hydrae could be around 0.01 to 0.05 solar masses per year. This rate is significantly lower than those previously reported in other studies, and our analysis suggests that magnetic forces play a critical role in reducing the mass loss rate in the planet-forming region of TW Hydrae. Ultimately, we believe that high-resolution radio observations in nearby star-forming regions will help to clarify the role of photoevaporation and magnetic forces in reducing the mass loss rate of planet-forming regions. Additionally, these observations may ultimately aid in understanding how photoevaporation affects the formation of planets in these regions. If these patterns are consistent across the sample of nearby star-forming regions, it could lead to the reduction of a planet's mass due to photoevaporation, as in the case of TW Hydrae, where the loss rate per unit mass could reach 0.01 percent per year. This reduction in mass could ultimately impact a planet's final mass and shape its formation. On the other hand, high-resolution radio observations may also help to clarify the role of photoevaporation in these regions and whether it contributes to the development of a planet's shape and size. It is possible that the mass loss due to photoevaporation in these regions could be compensated by the accumulation of solid particles, ultimately helping to clarify the role of photoevaporation

We introduce a new method, dynamically weighted inertial forward-backward (DWIFOB), to tackle structured monotone inclusion problems. By incorporating the forward-backward algorithm and the extrapolation technique from Anderson acceleration, along with a new projection update, DWIFOB enhances the convergence rate and regularity. Through analysis, we establish under mild assumptions that DWIFOB achieves a faster convergence rate compared to the forward-backward algorithm. Furthermore, DWIFOB maintains a globally convergent property when applied to a broad class of monotone inclusion problems. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we present numerical tests showing improvements over the forward-backward algorithm in terms of iteration count and total operations. Moreover, DWIFOB outperforms other accelerated methods, such as the proximal extra-gradient method and its strongly monotone counterpart, proximal cyclic algorithms, strongly monotone proximal shared-variability algorithms, and Tikhonov regularizations, through a new choice of parameters. Ultimately, DWIFOB emerges as a versatile and efficient algorithmic framework. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/AlessandroMaso/DWIFOB. Keywords: Monotone inclusion problems, forward-backward algorithm, Anderson acceleration, projection updates, iterative methods, convergence analysis, numerical tests, parameter choices, and performance evaluation. This research takes place within the Next-to-Minimal extension of the Standard Model (NMSSM), expanded by two singlet chiral superfields, along with a minimal set of extra neutrino singlet fields. By integrating the loop corrections into the one-loop decay width of the Higgs boson, we determine its precise mass range in this NMSSM framework, which incorporates three generations of standard type-I seesaw neutrino mechanisms. Within this model, the Higgs boson's properties align with those in the CMSSM, with certain constraints, and our study indicates that, in this case, the Higgs boson's total width is significantly less than its experimental limit. Furthermore, the Higgs boson's properties are largely unaffected by the superpartner masses, except for very high values, and the Higgs boson's mass and its total width are largely uncorrelated, which allows for a broader range of values, still within reach of future experiments. Our research also identifies the scenario in which the lightest R-parity non-conserving mediations have the greatest impact on the Higgs boson's properties. Additionally, the study into the flavour-violation in the complex doublet sector of the NMSSM reveals that its influence on the Higgs boson's properties is minimal. Lastly, the study indicates that, in this model, the parameter $\lambda_{\mathcal{N}}$ that governs the relationship between the singlet chiral superfields has a range of approximately $0.01\lambda_{\text{max}}$, where $\lambda_{\text{max}}$ is the upper bound of $\lambda$ and also serves as the upper bound of $\lambda_{\mathcal{N}}$. This model's constraint from the fermino mass difference, $\Delta m_f$, means that $\lambda$ cannot exceed approximately $0.64$, which implies that $\lambda_{\mathcal{N}}$ cannot exceed $\sim 6.28 \times 10^{-3}$, thereby severely limiting the range of the parameter $\lambda_{\mathcal{N}}$. The study further reveals that, in this model, the extra parameter, $\lambda_{\mathcal{N}}$, has a range that is nearly four orders of magnitude smaller than the range of the parameter $\lambda$ itself. This significant reduction in the range of the parameter, $\lambda_{\mathcal{N}}$, means that the neutrino masses are highly sensitive to the values of other parameters

Recent breakthroughs in Neural Design Automation have shown that deep neural networks can be trained to block patterns, eliminating the need for traditional design search methods. However, the process of training these networks from scratch remains time-consuming and often requires substantial expertise. To speed up neural design search, we've developed an innovative approach that allows existing deep neural networks to be adapted to new design blocks. The method requires only a high-level specification of the desired functionality. To facilitate this, we've created Property Directed Synthesis, a novel hardware compiler that generates multiple implementations of a specified behavior and trains a deep neural network to classify these designs based on their performance in simulating real workloads. The compiler's optimizations enable the learned patterns to generalize across multiple simulation scenarios, and experimental results show that existing networks can be adapted to new design blocks with only a 5% retraining cost. Federated Learning is a decentralized machine learning approach that allows clients to collaborate while maintaining their data's confidentiality, achieved through the collaboration of clients and a central server. Our research focuses on addressing the communication challenges in Federated Learning by introducing a new distillation technique known as FederatedDistill. Our evaluations, conducted using multiple datasets, demonstrate that FederatedDistill is resilient to various nonconvex and convex federated averaging scenarios and diverse federalist institutions. Additionally, we show that FederatedDistill offers significant advantages when combined with other advanced techniques such as Federated Learning with less frequently updated models and Federated Learning with stochastic gradient descent. Our research includes comprehensive code repositories for replicating our results on various datasets, federated learning setups, and models. A key challenge in Name Data Networking (NDN) lies in its coordination issue, which arises because naming conventions are determined by users with diverse objectives, thereby potentially leading to suboptimal outcomes. To address this challenge, research focuses on developing coordination mechanisms that facilitate dynamic decision-making among interconnected entities. This paper presents an innovative approach to resolving the coordination dilemma in NDN-based computing networks through a novel game-theoretic framework. By defining an optimal dynamic coordination problem as a repeated game with infinite horizons, we devise an intuitive decision-making model based on the concept of quasi-equilibrium. To achieve maximum long-term payoff outcomes, the first author's initial research explored dynamic strategies, which he later refined into a straightforward policy in this paper, demonstrating the dynamic stability of the refined strategy in specific scenarios. To extend the framework's applicability to general distributed systems, we devised two more policies, which were proven to be robust and efficient. This research is presented as a combination of two distinct papers, which will be jointly submitted to prominent journals in networking and distributed systems fields. A comprehensive simulation study validates the efficacy of our approaches, comparing them favorably to existing mechanisms. By imposing additional structural properties on the state transition matrix, we opened a new research area, exploring the implications on dynamic coordination policy and a novel concept called General- M. This new direction could lead to further innovation in coordinating complex systems. To facilitate replication, the source code of our simulation study is freely accessible on a public platform. To summarize, this research contributes two new ideas to the NDN coordination literature: the concept of quasi-equilibrium and the refined strategy policy, which address the coordination dilemma in specific and general scenarios, respectively. Additionally, we introduced two novel concepts: the refined strategy policy's robustness guarantee and the relationship between the transition matrix's properties and coordination, paving the way for future research. By freely providing the simulation code and publishing two distinct research papers, we strive to facilitate replication and exploration. This work is a significant contribution to the NDN coordination research, offering two fresh perspectives on dynamic coordination. This paper investigates the boundary stability of an elongated Euler-Bernoulli beam attached to a star-shaped structure with equally spaced points. We demonstrate that under certain conditions, specifically when the distance between each point is less than twice the beam's length, the entire system achieves stability. However, we also identify an essential limitation - that as the distance between these points decreases, the theoretical stability margin eventually becomes nonexistent below a critical length threshold. To further illustrate the principles behind this study, we generate a graphical comparison of theoretical and numerical stability margins. Further analysis reveals that these stability findings can be extended to more complex systems, such as multiple beams connected in series, under particular conditions. In contrast, we identify an unexpected instance of stability failure in a beam attached to three equally spaced points on a sphere. In an effort to explain these intriguing phenomena, we propose a simplified model based on the idea of effective boundary conditions. This model, derived from the original problem, sheds light on the complex interactions between spatial and temporal factors influencing stability. Ultimately, these findings contribute to our understanding of the intricate relationship between geometry and stability. The associated numerical data and PDE software code for this research are available via DOI: 10.5281/efis-eb-2022-19. Doi: 10.3938/z8-22-0001. Efis: efis-eb-2022-19.

This research explores how this phenomenon behaves in systems beyond the linear quark-meson model. Our findings indicate that as the chiral-asymmetry breaking term strengthens within these systems, 2nd-order changes transform into 1st-order phase transitions. Moreover, within the linear quark-meson model, incorporating chiral-asymmetry breaking terms results in the 2nd-order change disappearing as the strength of the terms increases, whereas the nature of the transition does not depend on the level of chiral-asymmetry breaking within more complex systems. Based on these results, the possibility of forming dense quark matter with distinct chiral and color phases under certain conditions exists. Our analysis also extends to systems beyond the linear quark-meson model, suggesting that 1st-order phase transitions may arise within these systems as well. Our results are further validated through comparison with existing studies. Our intended contribution is to initiate a discussion on the possible forms of dense quark matter, while also encouraging further research into higher-order theories. Our calculations according to the DFT framework indicate that the series of cadmium and mercury compounds, MTl$_4$Te$_3$, possess characteristics of topological insulators. With Te atoms forming a two-dimensional layer, the stability of these insulators in this series can be attributed to the telectrostatic interaction between Te and the cationic core of M (cadmium or mercury). This telectrostatic interaction gives rise to a strong te-ionic bonding in the Te plane, which is responsible for the energy gap at the Fermi level of these compounds. This te-ionic bonding is significantly influenced by the ionic radius of the cation, with mercury's larger radius resulting in a greater energy gap compared to cadmium. Notably, mercury-based compounds exhibit a higher te-ionic bonding energy and a greater energy gap, making them more stable as topological insulators. The properties of these compounds can be tailored through spin-splitting, achieved by introducing a moderate external magnetic field, which transforms them from a topological insulator to a band insulator. This phenomenon has been observed in the three-dimensional MTl$_4$Te$_3$ (M = Cd, Hg) compounds, which, despite varying properties, share a shared characteristic of being stable as topological insulators. This stability and their insulating properties at Fermi level along with te-ionic bonding make MTl$_4$Te$_3$ a unique series of te-ionic topological insulators. In multi-objective optimization problems with multiple competing objectives, evolutionary algorithms are widely utilized to generate a diverse set of sustainable and non-dominated solutions. Nonetheless, defining and implementing an objective function alongside user-provided preferences proves challenging. To address this issue, researchers have suggested utility function-based multi-objective evolutionary algorithms, which learn an aggregate objective function from user-specified preferences to facilitate global optimization. (Continues from previous research.) This study highlights the difficulties and limitations of utility function learning in the context of multi-objective optimization. Additionally, we introduce a new approach based on Tchebychev utility function and efficiently learn its parameters from user-provided preference matrices. Our proposed approach has been extensively tested using a wide range of benchmark problems and compared against established state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating its effectiveness and benefits. Importantly, our results show that this new approach outperforms the comparative methods in achieving optimal solutions and reducing computational costs. To validate the robustness of the learned utility function, we also examined its application to unknown problems and demonstrated its ability to adapt to new scenarios. Consistently, our results show that the proposed approach outperforms the comparative methods in achieving superior results. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed approach, we also demonstrated its application to a real-world engineering design problem, where user-provided preferences were utilized to optimize the design of digital circuits. Our results show that the proposed approach outperforms the comparative methods in achieving minimal computational costs while successfully optimizing the digital circuit design. In summary, this research highlights the difficulties of utility function learning in multi-objective optimization and introduces a new approach based on Tchebychev utility function that learns its parameters from user-provided preference matrices. Our results show that the proposed approach outperforms the comparative methods in achieving optimal solutions, reducing computational costs, and adapting to new scenarios. Additionally, we demonstrate its application to a real-world engineering design problem and achieve better results compared to state-of-the-art methods. In conclusion, this research contributes to the field of utility function learning in multi-objective optimization by highlighting its challenges and introducing novel and effective approaches that learn an aggregate objective function from user-provided preferences. These results may be useful for future research in utility function learning and multi-objective optimization. Valuable feedback from our collaborators guided and informed this research. Recent findings in reinforcement learning indicate that policies can be compromised using carefully crafted sequences of input, exploiting their reliance on past experiences. However, existing attacks on deep RL models require knowledge of the opponent's policy, dynamics of the environment, and reward function, making them impractical in real-world scenarios. Our study aims to rectify this by introducing a novel approach to attacking RL models without requiring any of these specifications. Our attack technique utilizes an RL model's internal predictions to cause maximal disruption, which we demonstrate through applications to grid-world and 3D robot navigation environments. Our evaluation shows that our attack can succeed in most cases across a range of settings. Our code can be accessed at https://github.com/jbarnesspain/blackbox-attacks-rl. Our tool can be accessed at https://github.com/RobotLoco/rl-attack-tool. Our video can be accessed at https://youtu.be/erQsS9R5R5g. Our paper has been accepted at IEEE Security and Privacy Forum. Two-dimensional periodic structures with symmorphic characteristics possess unique properties not found in other periodic systems. Within these structures, adjustable Dirac points can be found where the symmetry operations result in the convolution of the Hamiltonian wave functions, leading to the emergence of Dirac states. By adjusting the lattice parameters in a specific 2D symmorphic system, the energy at the Dirac points can be manipulated, potentially making these points disappear. This capability is rare in 2D periodic systems, and introducing perturbations to these systems typically locates Dirac points at the Fermi level. Our research demonstrates that adjusting certain parameters closes the Dirac points in one region and opens them in another, showcasing the unique properties of adjustable Dirac points in 2D symmorphic systems.

In reinforcement learning with risk considerations, learners must balance exploration and exploitation to discover an optimal policy while minimizing adverse outcomes. We investigate adaptive learning in risk-aware reinforcement learning with changing reward probabilities and penalties. Our research yields several key findings: First, we establish a dynamic regret bound for risk-aware reinforcement learning with changing reward probabilities and penalties. This regret bound declines at a rate proportional to the square root of the number of episodes and is only slightly worse than the optimal expectation-based regret. Second, we develop a sample-efficient algorithm that achieves this improved regret bound using a risk-aware exploration strategy. Third, we demonstrate that our algorithm is adaptive by allowing for changes in reward probability and penalty updates without affecting its performance. Lastly, we showcase the necessity of risk-aware exploration by illustrating a lower bound of at least $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ regret under a fixed risk setting. Our work presents novel contributions to risk-aware reinforcement learning, including a sample-efficient algorithm, adaptive learning capabilities, and a deeper understanding of the limits of reinforcement learning with risk considerations. Furthermore, our results imply that risk-aware exploration may be unnecessary in reinforcement learning with a fixed risk setting. The spectral dimension of a weighted graph is a concept that builds upon the Stochastic Navigation process introduced by Weitz in 2012. It can be determined by calculating the exponent of a power law in the rate at which a random walk covers the graph's scaled volume. On the other hand, the concept of Ahlfors-regular conformal dimension, developed by Bjorn and Bjorn et al in 2008-2014, is a measure of a metric space's irregularity. Calculating this dimension involves finding the minimum of the minimum exponents of local packing and covering over all possible scales. This study compares these two concepts on weighted graphs. It is shown that on a weighted graph with Ahlfors-regular conformal dimension α, the spectral dimension does not necessarily equal α. However, when α is an integer, equal to l, the spectral dimension lies within the interval [α/2, α] for a vast class of graphs, encompassing those with bounded volume growth and α > l. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that when α is a noninteger, equal to l, the spectral dimension can take any value within the interval [α/2, α] for a certain type of infinite graphs, encompassing those with volume growth tending towards infinity. It is proven that on a weighted tree with Ahlfors-regular conformal dimension α, the spectral dimension equals α. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that for any λ ≠ 1, equal to the weight of the tree, the spectral dimension also equals α. Finally, this study presents a vast class of infinite graphs, encompassing those with bounded volume growth and irregular conformal dimensions l and λ, in the 3-dimensional Euclidean space. It is proven that the spectral dimension of these graphs equals l and shows that the constraints of these graphs, having bounded volume growth, are necessary for determining the spectral dimension's value. We have investigated how the realization of higher-order topological correlations is impacted by this defect in systems featuring both bulk and edge states characteristic of fourth-order and third-order topological configurations. Our analysis, focusing on the quantum spin hall model with nearest-neighbor interactions, shows that the spin-vortex structure is resilient to the defect's influence in third-order topological cases but susceptible to modification in fourth-order topological scenarios. Specifically, for fourth-order topological cases with interactions exceeding nearest-neighbor range, the defect's effect is limited to the immediate vicinity of the defect site. Our results, obtained through both numerical and analytical evaluation, underscore the importance of interaction range in determining the stability of spin-vortex configurations around defects. Additionally, we have explored the associated correlation functions and spectrum modifications resulting from the defect's influence. Our findings indicate that the defect's presence does not preclude the realization of higher-order topological correlations but rather influences the distribution and stability of higher-order correlations throughout the system. Our investigation also sheds light on the defect's impact on realizations of quantum numbers, as adjusted for cases involving multiple interactions, and points out potential misconceptions in earlier topological classification studies that failed to consider interactions beyond nearest-neighbor range. Graph modeling has far-reaching implications in biomedicine due to its ability to accurately represent complex systems, encompassing biological entities interconnected through varied relationships. In addressing this critical field of study, the 2022 Graph Modeling and Simulation conference devoted a full session to the realm of biomedicine. This article summarizes the key findings presented in that session, featuring recent advances in using graph models to tackle significant issues in biomedicine. Specifically, the examples highlighted involve modeling of tumor ecosystems, drug repositioning, and simulating the spread of infectious diseases. A comprehensive review of the corresponding methods' underlying principles is also provided. These examples serve as a testament to the versatility and effectiveness of graph models in capturing the intricate nature of biological systems. As such, they serve as a valuable tool for data analysis, feature extraction, and decision-making across a wide range of applications in biomedicine. With their versatility and potential to tackle many more challenges, graph models will undoubtedly continue to play an essential role in the ongoing development of biomedical research and simulation. Our analysis compares and distinctively represents the relationships between these theories, and we also explore the relationship between PDC and DC with another theory called IOT (Inclusive Ordered Trees), as well as the scope of PDC and DC in terms of models of communication where the adversary can manipulate the channel. We show that in order to construct a communication model where the adversary can conceal data while maintaining its ability to determine input values, we must rely on techniques not available in the standard model. Moreover, we define a specific communication problem, known as the Majority Conflict problem, and demonstrate that it is solvable in PDC but not in PLO, and also solvable in DC but not in IOT. Inside the ATLAS detector, a lead-lead collision experiment at 5.02 TeV and proton-proton experiments at 13 TeV were conducted to examine the fragmentation patterns of high-transverse-momentum jets in both cases with and without the influence of nuclear interactions. This was achieved by comparing the fragmentation properties of jets from lead-lead and proton-proton collisions, specifically by measuring the ratios of inclusive jet spectra and the fragmentation functions of jets in lead-lead to proton-proton collisions. Two analysis methods were employed to analyse the data, resulting in similar fragmentation modifications for light-quark and gluon-dominated jets in both central and peripheral collisions, across all pseudorapidity ranges. This suggests that the observed modifications are primarily due to the effects of nuclear interactions, rather than changes in the quark-to-gluon jet composition. Furthermore, no collision system dependence was observed in the fragmentation distribution of jets above 50 GeV, which remains consistent with expectations based on perturbative QCD. This marks one of the first times that the fragmentation properties of gluon jets have been directly measured, providing crucial new insights into the colour-decomposition of proton-proton and nuclear interactions. By comparing and contrasting these results with calculations from the fragmentation functions of colour-neutral gluon phases, an internal alignment of the colour charges of these phases was determined to be less than 0.006 at 68% confidence, providing the most precise constraints to date on this parameter. The study also offers a new benchmark for the calculation of nuclear interaction effects in the final stages of heavy-ion collisions. By advancing our understanding of the colour interactions within protons and nuclei, this research paves the way for further breakthroughs in the fields of perturbative and non-perturbative physics. The findings are anticipated to be further refined with the analysis of a 2018 data set, which is set to reduce the measurement's uncertainty by a factor of three. This development will serve to further solidify the constraints on the colour-decomposition of proton-proton and nuclear interactions, effectively decreasing the upper limit on the alignment of the colour charges of these phases to less than 0.002 at 68% confidence. A class of conformal field theories can be characterized through scalable Schrödinger equations with conformal symmetry implications. These Schrödinger equations are interconnected with the Lax equations of a flat connection on a two-sphere surface, which reduces to the Euler-Arnold equations following a Lax representation. The conformal field theory's transition dynamics are defined by the Hamiltonian that underpins the Euler-Arnold equations. This study demonstrates that all central charge conformal field theories are derived from this overarching framework through a derivation based on the spectral action principle. The spectral action principle is motivated by a master field that is solution to a semi-metric equation, defining the metric of the conformal field theory space. The derivation is applicable to a broad spectrum of conformal field theories, encompassing both algebraic and Liouville theories. A key finding is that the spectral action principle natively incorporates the path-integral measure, precluding the need for an ad-hoc prescription. Furthermore, the central charge is inherently fixed as a consequence of the spectral action principle. The latter property is reflected in the non-linear realization of the conformal symmetry, effectively formulating the transition dynamics of the central charge. The conformal field theory's spectral action principle is analogous to the related concept in Horndeski gravity, where the central charge corresponds to the $\Loftel$ parameter. The solution derived from this spectral action principle is referred to as the spectral path integral. A crucial observation is that the spectral path integral is reinterpreted as a Gaussian path integral over the high-frequency components of the Schrödinger equation. This reinterpretation is facilitated by the semi-metric approach that decouples high-frequency and low-frequency components. Consequently, the low-frequency components are characterized by the Euler-Arnold equations, effectively defining the low-energy effective action. A novel algorithm called Complete Least Squares (CLS) is presented as a groundbreaking technique for accurate position calculation. CLS is an enhanced version of the Least Squares (LS) method, specifically tailored for Deep Sensor Networks (DSN) where sensor nodes use Deep Sensor Networks. The original Deep Sensor Networks approach relied on an iterative LS method but encountered issues due to local minima problems in the non-linear cost function. In contrast, CLS achieves optimal performance by converting the cost function into a full quadratic form, thereby bypassing the challenges associated with local minima. Furthermore, simulations conducted using artificially generated data reveal that CLS performs exceptionally well even in high noise conditions. In comparison with existing methods such as UBI, SBI, and LBI, CLS demonstrates remarkable accuracy and robustness. Notably, CLS demonstrates a distinctive "eye of fish" pattern in its 2D error trajectory, distinct from the "eye of dog" pattern seen with other methods. In addition to its remarkable performance, CLS's algorithmic structure shares striking similarities with the widely used Extended Kalman Filter (KF) method. In particular, both CLS and KF share a common objective, a full quadratic cost function, and similar mathematical structures, thereby establishing a strong connection between these two seemingly disparate algorithms. In support of the paper's findings, a comprehensive public repository of MATLAB code, along with corresponding results, has been made available. This structured repository is intended to facilitate future research and replication of the paper's findings. In essence, CLS presents a forward-thinking solution to the long-standing problem of position calculation in Deep Sensor Networks. In conclusion, CLS is poised to become a superior alternative to existing position estimation algorithms, offering superior accuracy and robustness. Moreover, CLS's novel connection to KF suggests vast potential for collaborative research and advancement of numerous algorithms. Ultimately, CLS is positioned to revolutionize the field of Deep Sensor Networks, thereby extending its reach to emerging technologies such as Deep Wireless Networks. In the words of the inventor, "This is CLS - it's time to give it to you!" Next-generation, high-perture detectors were utilized to collect data, which were then analyzed using the SFOS WW criterion to isolate events featuring two high-transverse momentum jets and two electrons or muons of identical sign.  Two production mechanisms were identified as contributing to same-sign W boson pairs: charged Higgs boson exchange, which generates a macromolecular gap, and the weak interaction itself, which is seen to produce weak macromolecular gaps in the mass of the W boson. GitHub is the leading platform for software development, housing an extensive repository of repositories. Maintaining and updating these repositories efficiently is critical, as it enables developers to ensure their software remains compatible with the latest operating systems, security protocols, and performance standards. Research into this aspect of software maintenance has gained traction, specifically a new approach called meta-maintenance. This approach analyzes the maintenance activities across multiple repositories shared on GitHub to identify patterns and predict future modifications. In a study of 3.48 million repositories, researchers applied meta-maintenance to assess its effectiveness, examining the variations in maintenance activities across repositories containing identical files. The analysis revealed that, on average, 11.3% of these files require modifications during maintenance activities and demonstrated a 25.6% increase in prediction accuracy compared to traditional maintenance methods. The benefits of meta-maintenance were also observed in a subset of high-performance projects, where its application yielded a 35.6% improvement in prediction accuracy. The findings of this study underscore the potential of meta-maintenance to enhance software maintenance activities. The associated data and computational resources are publicly available for further exploration.

In various fields such as computer vision, robotics, and statistical analysis, least squares methods are extensively used for estimating parameters based on noisy measurements. Although deterministic approaches exist for assessing the reliability of these estimates, current probabilistic methods that estimate their confidence levels are limited by the assumption that all data points are perfectly related to each other. In contrast, this research focuses on ensuring the reliability of least squares estimates when sample relationships are uncertain, influenced by noise. To resolve this issue, we introduce two novel techniques. First, a bounded confidence measure is developed for estimating parameters in linear regression. This measure provides a straightforward way to assess prediction errors. At the same time, a more precise Gaussian-based distribution is also proposed, which accommodates noisy samples while providing higher accuracy, at the cost of increased computational demands. Both theories are supported by numerical simulations. To verify the precision of these methods, we utilized a statistical test called the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. This research is significant because it identifies parameter estimation uncertainties due to noisy samples, which are often overlooked in previous studies. As a result, these techniques can be applied not only to linear regression but also to various other contexts, such as sparse recovery, higher-order least squares methods, and matrix decomposition. Additionally, these tools can be used for validating the outcomes of many other machine learning algorithms. Automated control systems rely on complex issues that Deep Reinforcement Learning can address, but certain difficulties like implementing determination policies and ensuring safety remain unresolved. A general issue with current Deep Reinforcement Learning techniques is that they struggle to scale beyond basic control issues. Additionally, most of these methods train a single policy to select actions in high-dimensional action spaces, which is problematic when specific action choices lead to safety hazards. To tackle these challenges, we introduce a two-staged approach that leverages large-scale reinforcement learning problems. This methodology involves a initial 'Determination Stage' that reduces the action space to manageable options based on environmental characteristics. Once the action space is optimized, a 'Execution Stage' fine-tunes the policy to select specific actions. To prevent unsafe behavior during the execution of learned policies, we implement a technique that produces a family of actions during determination stage. This allows an agent to select the most suitable action in real-time and our method is demonstrated to be safe and efficient through scalable simulations. Specifically, our approach successfully resolves control of a robotic manipulator with 10 joints and a robotic walking vehicle with 15 actuators, surpassing existing methods in efficiency and safety. Our two-staged approach generalizes to other difficult control issues and we provide an open-source implementation for the community to access. Further details are available at our website: https://two-staged-rl.github.io. Code repository: https://github.com/two-staged-rl/Two-Staged-RL. Video explanation: https://youtu.be/IX_9U3qR0wo.

This study is the second in a series focusing on the development of black holes through various mass ranges since the early universe. In contrast to our initial findings, which revealed how supermassive black holes grow through a controlled pattern, this outcome was unexpected due to its implications for supermassive black hole creation. According to our new findings, massive black holes, spanning a population that includes $\PU$-sharp and ultra-wide angle types, exhibit a distinct, stable, and consistent pattern of growth. We identified a fundamental, universal relationship that governs their behavior, where the rate of growth is directly proportional to their existing mass. This relationship holds across the broad spectrum of our studied mass range, from early universe predictions to observations of local black holes. In contrast to our initial predictions for low-mass black holes, our new outcomes show that they too follow a consistent pattern of growth, controlled by the surrounding cosmic environment. To overcome these challenges, researchers have developed a method of converting neural networks into readable, semi-interpretive models. These simplified models, derived from the original high-dimensional networks, mimic the input-to-output data transformation but with significantly reduced complexity. We have successfully applied this approach to translate IFS-Net neural networks, used for predicting inelastic neutron scattering spectra, into simplified models. This has allowed us to gain insight into the quasi-particle dynamics and how it relates to the electronic structure of the material. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), known for their exceptional properties of strength, corrosion resistance, and ability to form various variations, have become a rapidly evolving research area in materials science. To accelerate the optimization of HEAs, computational tools like machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) are being increasingly utilized to analyze their structure and behavior. This study reviews how ML and AI are enhancing research in HEAs, highlighting both the benefits and obstacles. It discusses the potential applications of these technologies in predicting material properties, understanding mechanical behavior, and simulating thermal treatments. To overcome existing limitations, such as incomplete data sets and a lack of fundamental theory, in-depth data analysis and a deeper understanding of the underlying physics are necessary. Ultimately, a combination of computational powers and human insights is required to develop more sophisticated models that can guide experimental investigations and aid materials design. This review is intended to provide an introductory overview of the current state of AI and ML in HEA research for scholars from both computational and experimental backgrounds. It also outlines future directions and invites readers to apply these technologies in advancing the field of materials science. This includes using data-driven techniques to develop new machine learning models and incorporating physical models to generate synthetic data sets that can inform AI-based algorithms. By leveraging these advanced tools, researchers can accelerate the development of innovative HEAs with unparalleled properties. Keywords: High-entropy alloys, machine learning, artificial intelligence, materials science, structure, propulsion systems, radiation environments, corrosion resistance, strength, materials design. Assuming the $T_{cc}^+$ discovered at LHCb is a $D^{\ast}D$ bound state, 
we examine its decay modes to this $D^{\ast}D\pi$ configuration. 
In a effective field theory framework, 
we have found that although the $T_{cc}^+$ can be described by an $L=0$ state, 
its decay modes do not significantly differ from those of a $J=3/2$ state. 
The most prominent decay channels involve the breaking of chiral symmetry and the presence of loop contributions, 
resulting in branching ratios of 18% (off-shell) to 22% (on-shell) for $D^{\ast}D\pi$ relative to $D^{\ast}D$. 
Furthermore, the distribution shapes for $D^{\ast}D\pi$ and $D^{\ast}D$ are comparable. 
Given the experimental challenges associated with identifying $T_{cc}^+$ decays, 
our study highlights the importance of examining potential background processes, 
such as those involving $D^{\ast}D\pi$ states that can arise from heavy-quark-spin partners and the $D^{\ast}D$ channel produced by a $T_{cc}^+$ state. 
In particular, we suggest that LHCb focus on $p_{T}$ distributions for $D^{\ast}$ mesons in events containing a $D^{\ast}$ meson and a proton, 
in order to establish the existence of the $T_{cc}^+$ and distinguish its signal from background processes. 

Due to the distinct nature of $T_{cc}^+$ production and decay,

Instead of focusing on events containing a $D^{\ast}$ meson and a $D^{\ast}$ meson,

This note outlines a theory-based approach to fitting parton distribution functions (PDFs). It focuses on predicting observable targets that can be calculated with theoretical PDF frameworks and compares them to experimental data. This process involves incorporating coefficients that represent the parameters of the PDFs, allowing for the fitting of their values to data. Notably, we make no assumptions about the form of the PDFs or their parameters; instead, they are solely constrained by the DGLAP evolution equations. We propose a novel fitting scheme that can be used with various PDF and NLO QCD frameworks, such as CT, NNPDF, and SCHUCHE, SCHUCHE with BChir, and SCHUCHE, SCHUCHE with BChir in conjunction with BALDIN-TEVAP. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to data from charged pion production and inclusive jet production. The results of this procedure are then compared to data from single inclusive pion, pi0 production, inclusive jet production, and top-quark pair production. The outcomes of this comparison reveal that the various PDF and NLO QCD frameworks produce somewhat similar results for the data in question. However, there are also some discrepancies between these predictions that may be attributed to factors such as differences in the PDFs themselves or the choice of NLO QCD corrections. One of the key strengths of ELKI lies in its adaptable and modular architecture, enabling users to easily tailor the library to suit their specific data analysis needs, as well as its generous licensing terms that foster a strong, community-driven development process. 

Throughout its development, the ELKI library has been systematically reviewed and documented to ensure maximum usability and readability. 

This release marks the fifth official announcement of a major release (0.7.x) and is accompanied by a comprehensive blog post available at http://elki.sourceforge.net/blog/2018-07-26-release-0.7.5.html.

We establish that in an acylindrically hyperbolic group G, random subgroups generated by independent random elements are nearly independent. Specifically, for any given pair of subgroups H_1 and H_2, randomly chosen within G, the probability that H_1 ∩ H_2 is exactly the trivial group exceeds 1/2 by a factor of at least 2^(1/8). Furthermore, this research extends existing findings by J. Sosna that a certain class of groups, also described as "nearly free," produce independent subgroup intersections. Our proof of this fact employs the framework developed by J. Behrstock and R. Zenteno. Additionally, our study reveals that the majority of subgroups in G are invariant under outer automorphisms, whereas others are dedicated to a specific representation of G. Understanding these latter subgroups, known as "loyal invariant subgroups," requires knowledge of G's combinatorial structure. To fully grasp these subgroups, we develop a procedure to identify them through a process of "loyal pairing." This concept of loyal invariant subgroups, paired with a certain type of subgroup known as "discriminatively finite," holds the potential for further exploration in group theory. To confirm the existence of loyal invariant subgroups in groups such as F_n and the free product of two finite groups, we combine existing proofs from multiple sources, including J. Behrstock, R. Zenteno, A. Jaikin-Zabjovskaya, N. Broemmel, A. Tran, and J. Eastabrook. Finally, based on preliminary numerical data, we hypothesize that a random subgroup of G is invariant under some automorphism with a probability of at least 1/2. A range of iterative methods can effectively solve problems involving constrained minimization under compressed sensing. While often these methods can be based on split Bregman algorithms, which guarantee convergence, using a fixed step size in these algorithms may result in slow convergence rates. In such cases, using different stabilization approaches can significantly improve the methods. In this work, we provide an in-depth examination of several stabilization techniques that, by accelerating convergence, make iterative methods even more efficient. We also compare these stabilization techniques in terms of their implementation, computational costs, and the conditions required for their validity. To demonstrate the effectiveness of these stabilization techniques, we test them on sparse recovery problems and MRI reconstruction problems. Additionally, we provide proof that these stabilization approaches not only accelerate convergence but also make the iterative methods stable and robust against deviations from the problem's prescribed step size. Furthermore, we extend the approaches to make use of the problem's geometry when available, thereby enhancing the stabilization. Numerous numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the benefits of these stabilization approaches, with results showing that they outperform other proposed methods in sparse recovery and MRI reconstruction. Furthermore, we provide code in MATLAB to facilitate the use of these stabilization techniques. We also provide an illustration of the techniques' action in a low-dose MRI reconstruction through an animated GIF. This investigation involves analyzing the Navier-Stokes equations for periodic initial conditions under maximum norm. Initially, we establish derivate estimates for scalar and vector fields in a periodic environment. Subsequently, we demonstrate the global solvability of these equations for all non-zero Reynolds numbers. Furthermore, we analyze how small perturbations in the force function impact the solution, revealing that a small change in the force results in a small change in the velocity field, quantified in terms of the Reynolds number and the size of the perturbation. Additionally, we explore the behavior of the velocity gradient in a periodic environment. Our study shows that the magnitude of the velocity gradient remains relatively small compared to its initial value, and we verify this by examining the eigenvalue problem associated with the linearized equations. Lastly, we analyze the high-frequency components of the velocity and its spatial variations in a periodic setting. Our work shows that these components decay at a rate determined by the Reynolds number and the frequency. These conclusions are supported by the solutions of the three-dimensional linear hyperbolic Cauchy problem in a torus. Importantly, our findings highlight that the nonlinear characteristics of the equations result in a relatively small exponent compared to the nonlinear analysis of the same problem in a torus. At the same time, the dissipation of the high-frequency components in a periodic setting remains relatively small compared to the dissipation of the high-frequency components in a torus. The recent proliferation of image synthesis methods based on implicit neural representations shows great potential for applying neural networks to model diverse visual content. These methods have significant advantages in creating the unknown sections of an image or generating entirely new images. Our research innovates by adapting these techniques to model the complex three-dimensional structures of yeast cells. Yeast cells are characterized by distinct organelles such as the nucleus, mitochondria, and vacuoles, which require accurate representation in order to understand their function and share knowledge across similar cells. Current 3D models often lack the precision needed for these purposes, but training a neural network to represent yeast cells and generate new, realistic models becomes challenging due to the scarcity of relevant data. Our solution involves developing Noise-Contrastive Distribution Learning (NCD-Learning), a novel training approach, in addition to introducing YChromosome, an interactive model development environment. Through extensive testing, YChromosome has demonstrated the ability to accurately place and represent various organelles in three-dimensional yeast cell models. Our results showcase the success of implicit neural representations in modeling intricate 3D structures like yeast cells, while also highlighting the need for creative and adaptable methodologies in applying this technique to complex data-scarce organisms. We introduce a type of flow, dubbed 'hard-drive dipoles,' that represent a convergence of stable periodic and non-periodic dynamics. This convergence is ensured by a new category of Markov chains, which we call 'non-retrograde.' Spectrograms effectively visualize the temporal variations in signal characteristics across different frequency ranges. Two key aspects of a spectrogram - the intensity, which indicates power levels, and the edge, which represents the boundary of significant amplitude - offer distinct insights into signal configurations. While most spectrogram analysis focuses on intensity, our approach explores the stochastic geometry of edge configurations. By defining an intrinsic metric on the spectrogram surface, we establish a probabilistic framework for examining signal properties. This methodology is applied to detect changes in signals with multiple components and to estimate parameters in signals with a single frequency component. Our analysis shows that, as the signal length increases, its edge configuration converges to a geometrically complex structure, akin to a fractal boundary. Specifically, our results reveal that the spectrogram surface features a multi-scale Gaussian Markov process, characterized by asymptotic stability and scalable parameters. These findings underpin a new theoretical structure for spectrogram analysis, complementing traditional methods based on intensity. By combining both approaches, spectrogram edge exploration can provide complementary insights, ultimately enhancing the detection of changes in signals with multiple components and parameter estimation in signals with a single frequency component. Our approach is applied to various signal types, including floating point, integer, and complex signals, and is accompanied by a range of supporting experiments and numerical data. Additionally, we introduce a new software package, SPECTRA, for spectrogram edge analysis, as well as a range of example notebooks and numerical data sets available online. Random acceleration algorithms are commonly employed in N-body simulations for equating the dynamics of gravitational and random forces. Although they seem simplistic, they facilitate a straightforward correlation of the motion of celestial bodies in models with and without chaos. The implementation of such an algorithm in the REBOUND N-body simulation code is described, along with its execution. The authors analyze the outcomes of this algorithm, particularly its potential for generating equitable initial conditions in planetary models, leveraging REBOUND's performance as a high-speed, specialized code. The paper further explores random acceleration experiments as a means of investigating the dependence of the quaternary planetary system's structure on this type of forcing, utilizing the results of an experiment involving $10^{8}$ iterations. The authors discovered that random acceleration can generate planetary ratios comparable to those observed in our solar system, notably the 3:2 resonance. Moreover, they found the existence of various patterns and constraints governing the quaternary structure, which they seek to exploit for generating realistic planetary configurations in the future. The REBOUND package, along with the underlying code used in this research, is freely accessible at https://rebound.readthedocs.io/en/stable/ and https://dx.doi.org/10.5202/iads.5.211.

In systems with electronic flat bands, quantum properties such as superconductivity, magnetism, and topological orders are frequently observed. THz radiation enables the precise stimulation of vibrational frequencies within molecules and crystals, making it possible to study its influence on related phenomena. When applied to electronic systems, THz radiation interacts with both the electrons and the stimulated phonons, leading to the induction of pure spin currents. Researchers have observed that in some materials, the interaction with THz radiation results in the creation of spin-vibronic states. Currently, there are only a few theoretical models available to describe these interactions, with most simplifying the electron-phonon coupling and ignoring the inertia of electrons and phonons. In contrast, our proposed model treats all interactions equally, simulating the dynamic stimulation of phonons and electrons simultaneously. In the case of a doped Dirac soliton in a graphene-like system, the dynamic interaction leads to the separation of electrons and holes, while in a molecular complex, the interaction induces the separation of spin and charge. The separation is a general outcome when the inertial effect is significant, differing from static electron-phonon interactions. In static conditions, electrons are localized around the phonon cloud, whereas in our scenario, the situation is reversed - the phonon cloud is localized around the electrons. The unique properties of graphene, graphene bilayers, and other materials with graphene-like properties make them particularly suitable for the study of dynamic interactions. Furthermore, we propose that blue SHG (second-harmonic generation) could serve as a powerful tool to investigate electron-phonon coupling in pumped laser systems. By employing blue SHG, it becomes possible to stimulate phonons while simultaneously interacting with electrons, thereby enabling the exploration of inertia effects, an aspect previously unexplored in electron-phonon coupling. In conclusion, we have demonstrated that the simulation of dynamic interactions offers a broader range of possibilities than static interactions, thereby holding greater promise for the development of innovative technologies. Ultimately, our understanding of these interactions may lead to breakthroughs in the field of quantum computing. In an quantum world, the simulation of dynamic interactions may enable the creation of quantum gates resistant to errors, while also facilitating the development of quantum algorithms capable of solving complex problems, such as factoring large numbers. In an engineering context, we have demonstrated that dynamic interactions can be utilized to develop devices for high-speed, high-frequency, and scalable optoelectronic applications. In an intrinsic graphene system, we have shown that the simulation of dynamic interactions results in the creation of spin-vibrons, while also making the system more sensitive to THz radiation, thereby expanding its energy spectrum. This included channel 1 (0.450 μm) and channel 2 (0.520 μm) spectral reflectance values from the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES-16). We also observed new dimensions emerged when utilizing both satellite channels, contrasting with individual spectral responses. Effective reduction was achieved with minimal information loss when projecting original data onto our learned representations. Theoretical models of location tracking privacy evaluate how hiding one's trajectory affects privacy when releasing aggregated data. A novel framework, based on conditional priors, measures privacy as the divergence between actual and estimated distribution of a released variable. This analysis leads to a more accurate privacy assessment compared to previous methods. By applying this framework to release mechanisms that report location data with Gaussian and Cauchy errors, the study derived closed-form expressions for privacy. Specifically, it demonstrated that releasing data with Gaussian error results in minimal privacy gains, whereas introducing Cauchy error provides significant privacy enhancements, particularly when incorporating prior knowledge. Furthermore, the research investigated how to optimize noise added to location data for maximum privacy, yielding an optimal variance value under a logarithmic condition. A computational experiment confirmed that, in the absence of prior information, releasing data with uniform or Gaussian error within a specified bound yields comparable results, whereas incorporating prior knowledge enables more precise analysis and better performance. Lastly, the study identified potential research directions and suggested future areas of investigation. A related code can be accessed at https://github.com/EstefanyA/Location-Tracking-Privacy.
