Roughly ten years ago, studies on resting-state fMRI began using independent component analysis to investigate brain connectivity. Since then, the method's popularity has continued to grow, with more than 500 such studies published to date. Despite widespread use, there is a lack of comprehensive evaluation and guidance on how to accurately analyze data in a multisite setting, especially when it comes to determining the number of dimensions for estimation and group prediction. To address this, we developed and implemented a stochastic approach for estimating multiscale connectivity structures in a resting-state fMRI dataset obtained from multiple sites, with and without shared tasks. Our method involves a Bayesian model selection metric to determine the optimal number of dimensions for the connectivity structure, and subsequent prediction results show that our approach outperforms traditional methods. Using a high-performance computing cluster, we simulated a distribution of results by varying random seed values, and found that our method produces less variable results compared to other techniques. Our research demonstrates the feasibility and accuracy of our approach, and we make available a publicly accessible version of the code and data, in the hopes that it may aid in facilitating reproducible research in the field of brain connectivity studies. A correspondence address is provided at the end of the manuscript for those interested in requesting access to the data and code. Furthermore, we highlight potential areas for further research and note the inherent complexities and challenges in multilevel brain connectivity data analysis. In this study, we have investigated how pressure affects the electronic density of states at the Fermi level in H$_3$S hydride, a material known to undergo a transition to superconductivity under high pressure. Using a combination of density functional theory and the lattice dynamics tool, we analyzed the impact of lattice vibrations on the electronic structure of H$_3$S. Our results, obtained through a double frequency-dependent density functional approach, reveal that both mechanical and vibrational influences contribute to a positive isotope effect in H$_3$S. Furthermore, we observed that the increased electronic density of states at the Fermi level due to both mechanisms stabilizes the superconducting transition, leading to a critical temperature of approximately 55 K when the isotopic mass difference is set at 4. Additionally, we noted that the speed of pressure application has a significant impact on the electronic density of states at the Fermi level, as evidenced by the contact interaction calculations. Our findings indicate that the acceleration of pressure application suppresses the speed at which the electronic density of states changes in response to pressure, thereby hindering the superconducting transition. Our analysis also identifies a van Hove singularity in the electronic density of states of H$_3$S at approximately 4.5 eV, which is consistent with similar features observed in other group-VII hydrides under high pressure. Our study provides a theoretical basis for the experiments aiming to achieve superconductivity in H$_3$S at high pressures. Additionally, we have reported a novel finding that the acceleration of pressure application can alter the location of this van Hove singularity, as well as the location of a potential barrier that the trio of H$_2$, HN, and HS hydrides undergo as they gain or lose a hydrogen atom. Our results indicate that the dynamics of lattice vibrations play a critical role in these processes, as evidenced by our calculations of the phonon frequencies and their influences on the electronic structure of these materials. Our analysis provides a theoretical understanding of the experiments aiming to achieve superconductivity in these materials as well. Fisher's mean effect size is often misunderstood and unnecessary, allowing other measures such as Hedges' difference effect to emerge. However, the mean effect size retains importance in Bayesian analysis, particularly for estimating the standard deviation of effect sizes, which is necessary for calculating Bayes factors. The choice of effect size measure does influence the results but only in cases where one measure is correlated with a study-specific parameter. In contrast, the mean effect size is unaffected by such correlations. Consequently, researchers should carefully consider which effect size to use when applying Fisher's method for inference. Furthermore, our results highlight several areas for improvement in the application of Fisher's method. Firstly, researchers should not assume independence of effect sizes as this assumption can lead to inaccurate inference. Relying solely on the mean effect size may also fail to utilize the information contained within individual studies. Finally, researchers should not assume that distributions of effect sizes are uniform as this can result in inaccurate Bayes factors. Estimating the prior distribution based on the mean effect size can lead to particularly inaccurate results. Conversely, when effect sizes are normally distributed and independent, the mean effect size is an accurate representation of the prior distribution, allowing researchers to make accurate inferences. Ultimately, researchers are cautioned against relying on simplistic implementations of Fisher's method and should instead customize approaches to suit their specific needs. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/JamesWTeo/FisherMeanCustomised. Additionally, a detailed tutorial on applying Fisher's method can be found at https://jameswteo.github.io/FisherMeanCustomised/ tutorial/fisher_mean_customised.html. We have also established a community on NetForum for those interested in discussing and refining methods for applying Fisher's method in inference. The forum can be accessed at the following link: https://netforum.cogsci.nl/default.asp?index=2&folder=221. Future human explorations of Mars and other planetary bodies with low gravity environments will rely on wearable powered exoskeletons to assist in walking. Conventional designs based on actuation through electric motors may not be sufficient, especially considering the additional challenges posed by low gravity. Investigating the potential benefits of using propulsion systems to assist in walking, such as hot air ovens or cold gas thrusters, could lead to more efficient designs. This research focuses on evaluating the use of propulsion systems as energy sources for bipedal movement. Thermodynamic analysis of these systems reveals that they could provide a significant advantage in terms of energy output when compared to conventional electric actuation. A custom-made bipedal robot was developed to test these propulsion systems in a gravity simulation chamber that mimics the gravitational conditions on Mars. Successful trials using hot air ovens as actuators have shown that these systems can significantly improve walking efficiency and stability. Ongoing evaluations using cold gas thrusters are promising, with the potential to also increase the robot's range by allowing it to move its legs in relation to its center of gravity. This research will contribute to the creation of more efficient powered exoskeletons capable of withstanding the stresses of low gravity environments. Additionally, the sturdiness-enhancing capabilities of propulsion-assisted bipedal movement could be applicable to other fields, such as robotics and transportation. Directly relying on images leads to location uncertainty due to varying lighting and scene patterns changing the image features. This research demonstrates that using 3D surfel maps, which break down scenes into coherent geometric units, significantly improves visual relocalization. By utilizing these maps, relocalization reduces dependence on image features and incorporates prior knowledge of the scene. To further enhance accuracy, this study integrates learned features from a geometrically-aware multi-scale network into the traditional SURF feature extractor. Comprehensive tests in diverse outdoor settings reveal that the proposed method achieves higher success rates and faster computation times compared to existing techniques. Notably, using the constructed 3D surfel map alone allows for 90% accurate relocalization without further image information. Label ambiguity is a significant challenge in semi-supervised learning, particularly in distributed federated learning environments where data comes from various sources with different labeling practices. This research aims to address label ambiguity in federated semi-supervised learning by first identifying and quantifying label uncertainty on each participant's node. A novel framework is then proposed to integrate label ambiguity into the model, ensuring consistent results across different labeling practices. Through theoretical analysis, the non-convexity impact of label ambiguity on the joint optimization problem is understood. To circumvent this challenge, a customized federated semi-supervised learning approach is developed, comprising two phases: an initial round of centralized training to reduce label ambiguity and improve overall performance, followed by decentralized training to minimize communication costs. The proposed approach is evaluated in simulation-based experiments across different labeling practices, demonstrating improved accuracy and reduced communication costs. We use these measures to understand slow convergence in one process (the 'test process') to its quasi-stationary counterpart (the 'Q-process). We find that previous criteria for determining if a test process converges to its Q-process are either too lenient or too restrictive. We discuss the limitations of existing methods for calculating the Q-process and explore what changes could make a test process easier to converge to its Q-process. This research is part of a larger effort to create realistic statistical models of events in areas such as biology, medicine, finance, and traffic studies. In contrast, test processes with constantly occurring events but varying durations are more difficult to converge to their Q-processes. In emergency medicine, decision-making often relies heavily on rapid, real-time judgments due to time-critical situations and high-pressure environments. Research in emergency medicine highlights the significance of timely interventions, emphasizing the need to understand how providers' decision times and priority ordering are influenced by the duration of interventions. This study aims to improve emergency medical interventions by identifying the most efficient duration that influences decision-making and priority allocation. Using a simulation-based approach with 129 emergency medicine residents who evaluated patient scenarios, we found that, on average, emergency medicine residents take around 15 seconds to process new information in the emergency department. Notably, we observed two distinct patterns of response curves for intervention durations: longer durations led to consistently lower decision times and priority scores in the first pattern, whereas, in the second pattern, only very long durations resulted in consistently lower decision times and priority scores. Ultimately, we recommend that emergency medicine interventions aim to strike a balance between duration and decision-making complexity to effectively inform emergency medical interventions. This research provides a framework and a typical response curve model that can be utilized for emergency medicine intervention development, showcasing its potential to improve clinical decision-making in emergency settings. Keywords: Emergency medicine, Intervention duration, Medical decision-making, Simulation-based approach, Response curves.

In highly complex systems, collaboration among multiple agents is necessary to tackle a wide range of challenges. This research paper demonstrates the capability of multi-agent collaboration for solving local coverage issues through standard robot networks with limited computation and communication capabilities. We show that two robots with line-of-sight and restricted vision can successfully cover an area by exchanging signal strength information. This approach employs signal strength as the main metric for navigation and collision avoidance. Following an initial signal exchange, each robot makes independent decisions based on local information, allowing them to operate independently without further communication. As a result, an area is efficiently covered by the robots in a distributed manner. Additionally, we analyzed and estimated the computational costs of these decisions. Experimental trials confirmed the effectiveness of this method in real-world tests. This research has positive implications for space exploration missions where robots with limited capabilities may be deployed. An example video of the experiment is available at https://youtu.be/7kpxTTp_6Gk. (In English)

A crucial aspect of Autodrive technology is accurately localizing and tracking vehicles in real-time, which is typically achieved through multiple reliable beacon vehicles equipped with GPS. However, in the event of beacons failing or experiencing interference, this approach becomes ineffective, resulting in a location service outage that could last for an extended period. As such, there is a pressing need to develop an algorithm that can quickly adapt to beacon failures and provide accurate location information within a short timeframe. In light of this challenge, this research presents a pioneering solution grounded in the principles of communication transfer. By estimating the location of a vehicle based on signal transfers between vehicles and beacons, this algorithm is capable of restoring location services immediately following failures. Furthermore, this approach can also pinpoint the beacon that has malfunctioned, thereby enabling proactive measures to be taken. Simulations conducted using real-world data revealed that this algorithm is adaptable across various scenarios, including rapid failures and partial outages, with an average location error of less than 5 meters. Importantly, this algorithm's processing time is under 20 milliseconds, making it suitable for real-time applications. Experimental field tests validated the effectiveness of this algorithm at restoring location services immediately following failures. Therefore, this paper confirms that this algorithm remains a resilient solution for localizing and tracking vehicles in the most demanding of scenarios. While traditional methods focus on treating these data points as ordinary observations, this work reveals that they can be efficiently ranked using a simplified approach based on the Isometric Log-Ratio transformation. By applying this change of variable, we redefine the depth and show that it adheres to essential properties, such as depth order and the extreme value properties, without requiring the computationally intensive step of density estimation. The new approach enables fast and precise calculations even for large datasets, reducing the time complexity from O(n^2) to O(n). We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through comparisons with alternative pointwise depth measures. Furthermore, we extend the concept of depth to functional regression models, revealing that the efficiency of this method is directly linked to the performance of the underlying model. The findings of our simulations confirm that this method surpasses the efficiency of the competing depth measures. Model Architecture
Our proposed model builds upon the existing Transcriptor RNN, widely employed in text recognition tasks. We make two key modifications to support regular expressions in recognition: 

1.  Label Embeddings: To effectively incorporate RE-based labels, we modify the label embedding module by using a separate vector for each label rather than a shared space. This allows closer alignment between input visual features and label information.

2.  Decoding: The standard Transcriptor RNN uses a greedy decoding method. We substitute this with an algorithm that explores multiple hypotheses before making a final prediction. Specifically, at each step, it predicts a set of future token probabilities, allowing for better structure recognition.

Prior Distribution over Regular Expressions
To enhance structured text recognition, we introduce a prior distribution over regular expressions. This is done through a separate network that generates possible RE-based labels given the initial input image features. The predicted distribution then acts as an additional heuristic in the decoding algorithm to guide recognition.

Developing a visual language model that can automatically create SQL queries from written descriptions in a database query language is an intricate task, requiring broad understanding of both domains.  To overcome the challenges of learning two distinct languages, we propose a new model that learns a cross-language translation through an auxiliary task.  By using this auxiliary translation, we enable our primary model to generate more accurate SQL queries in the target domain, according to written descriptions in the source domain.  Our model can be trained in a unsupervised setting, without requiring labeled data for the target language, by using data from the source domain.  Experiments conducted on datasets from three independent sources reveal our model outperforms state-of-the-art end-to-end models in translating SQL queries from additional domains.  Additionally, we introduce two new evaluation metrics to assess visual reasoning and linguistic translation skills in database query languages.  Our model achieves superior performance in both new metrics and shows its ability to generalize to novel domains.  For more information, you can check our project page at https://github.com/asharathp/VLDBQL. In a scenario of trust uncertainty, individuals become hesitant to express their genuine beliefs about social hierarchies, leading to a phenomenon of "preference shift". This concept is rooted in Social Learning Theory (SLT), which suggests people learn from others to form their opinions. However, the traditional approach to modeling opinion dynamics assumes the existence of a clear social structure, whereas in reality, it often evolves simultaneously with opinion shifts.

To tackle this challenge, we develop a novel theoretical framework combining the ideas of structural equilibrium and opinion dynamics. The framework is based on two key components - the concept of limited confidence, which stems from preferential shift, and a coupled opinion shift based on social learner interactions. Through the analysis of our theoretical model, we demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of an equilibrium solution. Furthermore, we classify opinions dynamics into two distinct phases: in the initial stage, opinions spread rapidly throughout the network; in contrast, the slow spread in the later stage is predominantly driven by the dynamics of structural equilibrium. The mathematical proof of our theory is accompanied by numerical simulations and an empirical study, which demonstrates the relevance of our theoretical framework in a real-world setting. The results of these experiments confirm that individuals do experience preference shift and express lower levels of limited confidence when they belong to a flat social network rather than a hierarchical one. The developed theory is then used to forecast the ongoing trend of opinion dynamics. In summary, we contribute a novel theoretical framework that captures the dynamic interplay between opinion shifts and structural changes, while also providing practical applications and future research directions. Despite the importance of RNA for numerous cellular processes, the causes and consequences of these delays are not well understood.  Recent advances in live-cell imaging and single-molecule localization microscopy have provided insight into transcription rates and patterns, but the small population sizes in live cells often limit precision.  To overcome these challenges, researchers used genome-wide approaches combining high-resolution mapping of transcription sites with quantitative measurement of RNA copy numbers.  By switching on transcriptional activity in specific regions of the genome, researchers discovered that the production of certain genes is delayed relative to others.  Through computational modeling, the researchers found that a key factor influencing these delays is the structure of the chromatin, with narrower chromatin packing allowing for faster transcription access.  Experimentally verifying the role of chromatin modifications in transcription rates, the researchers discovered that acetylation of certain lysines in the promoter regions of delayed genes leads to increased transcriptional activity.  These findings suggest that the complex interplay between chromatin structure and the dynamic nature of genome packing plays a crucial role in controlling RNA production in cells.  This knowledge could potentially lead to new therapeutic strategies for manipulating gene expression.  Additionally, the researchers developed a mathematical model for incorporating transcriptional delays based on chromatin structure, utilizing a stochastic approach that accounts for uncertainties in measurements.  This model, when applied to real data, accurately predicts lags in RNA production and provides a framework for further analysis and exploration. This study provides a framework for future investigation into the underlying causes and the wide-range implications of transcriptional delays in cells. are explored in this review, focusing particularly on the most well-known examples, 
Chiral Yang-Mills theory and Chiral Dirac-Bernoulli theory. For Yang-Mills theory, 
the dual theory is discussed in detail, along with an analysis of the mapping between 
microscopic and macroscopic properties. In contrast, the dual theory to Dirac-Bernoulli 
is shown to be inconsistent when quantized. This review utilizes a graph theoretical 
framework that enables the efficient computation of thermodynamic properties. In the 
case of Yang-Mills theory, the dual theory provides an analytically soluble description 
of the model, while for Dirac-Bernoulli, the dual theory delivers an extremely accurate 
approximation. Other chiral gauge theories are examined, including a general model with 
coupled matter fields, for which the dual theory is shown to be in excellent agreement 
with numerical simulations. Finally, the prospects and constraints for establishing 
non-supersymmetric dualities are critically assessed. In particular, the utility of 
non-supersymmetric dualities as a means of obtaining an ab initio derivation of supergravity 
from super Yang-Mills theory is explored. While some challenges to construction can be 
overcome, others appear insurmountable. Ultimately, the potential of chiral gauge 
theories to contribute to the broader field of AdS/CFT correspondence is realized through 
the example of Holographic Causal Perturbation Theory. This framework, derived independently 
from the dual theory of Yang-Mills, shares striking parallels with the dual theory of 
Dirac-Bernoulli. This review is a distilled version of a longer review article first published 
in 2019, with additional developments incorporated from 2020-2021. Due to space constraints,

In complex graphical models, exact computation of marginal matching poses a significant challenge, largely due to the high computational demands of current methods. This paper introduces a breakthrough technique, referred to as 'Brief Function Depiction (BFD)', which dramatically reduces the computational load. The BFD technique leverages the 'temporal shift operator' to simplify the representation of recursive formulas, thereby enabling direct and efficient mapping of temporal operators to circuit components. This advancement enables the development of an optimal algorithm for MPE within polynomial time, along with enhanced sampling methods and robust optimization techniques, all of which outperform existing strategies. The proposed BFD technique is versatile, adaptable to various types of recursive formulas and can be applied with minimal modifications to other problem-solving approaches. We examine the global dynamics of shear thickening transitions in viscoelastic materials across various geometries, discovering that the onset of shear thickening is consistently forecasted by a simple dimensionless critical stress criterion, independent of material nonlinearity. The stress threshold for shear thickening is higher than in purely elastic materials and is correlated with the shear rate at which it occurs, as well as with the material's initial linear viscosity. The critical stress for shear thickening scales inversely with the material's initial linear viscosity, and the shear rate at which it occurs scales inversely with the material's inertia. We further observe that when shear thickening occurs, the material's overall stress and strain distribution becomes self-similar, and that this phenomenon is governed by a balance between inertial and nonlinear viscous forces. In contrast to other types of rheological transitions, such as shear thinning, the material's overall stress and strain history exhibit little memory of its pre-shear state. Rather, the onset of shear thickening is largely forecasted by global measures of the shear flow's velocity profile, and can be understood through simple scaling based on the material's inherent physics. Moreover, we find that the sudden loss of fluidity at the onset of shear thickening is accompanied by a dramatic reduction in the material's overall entropy production. In consequence, we suggest that the shear thickening transition may be associated with a soft and fragile nature in materials science terminology. Finally, we present theoretical arguments suggesting that shear thickening may always be accompanied by a shear elastic softening at its onset, and that the material's overall shear elastic response becomes largely determined by the shear rate at which it occurs. In consequence, we find that the material's overall stress and strain history exhibit a universal, geometric scaling based on the type of flow geometry in which it occurs. The material's stress and strain responses in plane and circular geometries become completely determined by the stress threshold for shear thickening, and can be predicted from a single experiment in which the material is subjected to shear thinning. Similarly, the material's overall stress and strain responses in channel and cone flows become completely determined by the stress threshold for shear thickening, and can be predicted from a single experiment in which the material is subjected to shear thinning. In consequence, we find that the material's overall stress and strain responses in any type of flow can be predicted from a single experiment in which the material is subjected to shear thinning, provided that the stress threshold for shear thickening is known. Climate patterns often exhibit intricate connections with local and global factors, spanning various time scales. Diminution techniques in climate dynamics analyze these patterns on different spatial or temporal scales, searching for self-similar features at larger or smaller sizes. This study summarizes recent developments in climate dimension analysis, covering dimension estimates, long-range interference patterns, and long-term climate forecasting. It also explores the application of diminution techniques in studying climate phenomena, such as turbulent flows, ocean currents, and snowfall patterns, as well as their use in forecasting solar activity and temperature fluctuations. Showcasing the diversity of diminution techniques in climate studies, this review delves into methods like multifractal analysis, fractional Brownian motion, and mixed self-similar random functions. These techniques hold promise for advancing climate research and understanding complex dimensionality in the Earth's atmosphere and oceans. As a result, this field is expected to continue growing in the near future. Compositional data analysis is a type of statistical analysis that focuses on complex, multi-component data sets, which are prevalent in social sciences, geochemistry and microbiome research. Due to the constraints of such data sets, which have a zero sum property, specific mathematical operations must be applied when manipulating them. Proportion-based transformations are commonly used but pose challenges for linear algebra calculations. In this work, we explore alternative compositions that enable linear algebra and machine learning techniques like regression, principal component analysis and clustering to be utilized effectively. Our method, based on log composition, enables smooth visualization of compositional data and allows for the interpretation of resulting models through the use of partial dependence plots. Additionally, we have developed a set of open-source tools that incorporate these concepts to facilitate easy analysis of compositional data sets. Our methodology is demonstrated through a range of examples, which highlight the benefits of our approach in comparing performance and understanding feature importance in both predictive and exploratory contexts. The exoplanet population's characteristics, particularly in the mid-range mass segment ($\sim 0.1\,M_{J}\,M_{\odot}$), are still poorly understood. This population's assessment is complicated by detection biases affecting planets in this mass area. To investigate these biases, researchers used the CORALIE/HARPS radial velocity dataset composed of $\sim 800$ systems with $\sim 800$ planets, focusing on the transition zone ($0.1\,R_{\odot}$) where Saturn mass planets ($\sim 0.05\,M_{J}\,M_{odot}$) are likely to be orbiting within or near the habitable zone. By analyzing dimensionality-reduced and volumetrically normalized projections of their data, they discovered an absence of planets with masses between $\sim 0.1\,M_{\odot}$ and $\sim 0.25\,M_{\odot}$ orbiting closer than $\sim 3\,R_{\odot}$. This phenomenon does not exist for less massive planets. They propose that the lack of mid-range mass planets in their sample indicates a high rate of destruction through gravitational interactions with other planets in the system, especially by massive planets with masses similar to those of Jupiter. As a result, the team concludes that the probability of finding habitable-zone planets with masses similar to those of Saturn is higher than expected. Additionally, they suggest that such planetary systems are often dominated by one or several massive planets with masses similar to those of Jupiter. This research is likely to be consistent with recent findings of the TESSGI study and the expected outcomes of the PLATO mission. Finally, the team estimates that to eliminate detection biases affecting mid-range mass planets, a radial velocity dataset with at least $\sim 5000$ systems and extending to larger planetary masses would be required. This means that future radial velocity surveys may need to be expanded beyond their current scope to accurately assess the population's characteristics of planets in this mass area. This research does not rule out the presence of significant population gaps at smaller masses, as evidenced by previous studies on super-Earths. It examines the parameter influence, convergence, and the role of optimal transport in global averaging methods, such as Santos and Samorodnitsky's recent approach. This leads to a simplified form of their method using a specific averaging process, and further connects it to other global averaging techniques. It also reveals a fundamental issue with Santos and Samorodnitsky's approach that affects its practical application. Building on previous work by Birkhuis and Ressel, this study introduces enhanced global averaging methods that overcome existing limitations. Notably, it demonstrates the applicability of optimal transport theory to global averaging, and shows how to achieve low computational complexity for large datasets. This is achieved by replacing a non-differentiable optimal transport cost function with a more efficient and manageable alternative. This reformulation enables the use of closed-form solutions for optimal transport equations, and improves the convergence rate of iteration algorithms. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of these methods. Specifically, it shows that the new methods achieve comparable results to existing techniques while reducing computational time. This is illustrated through a study of clustering synthetic data, which reveals the new methods outperformed existing ones in predicting cluster numbers. Additionally, it shows the new methods successfully applied to the Bump dataset. This research contributes to our understanding of global averaging by generalizing previous work, connecting distinct approaches, and introducing enhanced methods that extend previous findings. Crucially, it shows global averaging can be efficiently applied to large datasets while achieving comparable results to existing techniques. Key algorithms developed in this study are available for public use. Additionally, the associated code and numerical studies are accessible on a dedicated GitHub platform. A study conducted by LaMassa et al. (2019) revealed that active galactic nuclei, classified as radio-loud or quiet, exhibit distinct characteristics regarding their host galaxies. In this investigation, we analyze a separate aspect of active galaxies, focusing on whether the shape and orientation of these nuclei impact their various spectral types. To accomplish this, we derive an appropriate parameterization for the axis of rotation, thereby allowing us to define a flat rotational plane in the Euclidean space of four dimensions, with the additional capability of generalizing the standard parameterization for the plane when it rotates around a central point. Deep learning models are widely used for pixel-level image classification, known as semantic segmentation. Most approaches initially engage in pre-training, a cost-free step that prepares the network with essential skills. Traditional methods typically utilize publicly available datasets like the ImageNet Challenge. However, due to the relatively simple nature of these images, researchers have turned to more complex datasets. Although effective, these larger pre-training tasks come at a significant cost for modern computing systems. Consequently, researchers are now exploring alternative approaches, such as using depth assessment or other tasks, to pre-train their networks. Our study assesses the potential of using depth assessment as an unsupervised pre-training method for semantic segmentation. Notably, depth assessment is closely related to certain types of real-world applications, such as autonomous driving, where 3D environmental information would be beneficial. To this end, we investigate depth assessment's potential for enhancing 2D semantic segmentation performance through pre-training. Our approach simply modifies the final output layer of a model to predict 3D depth values instead of class labels. By doing so, we discover that models pre-trained on large-scale depth datasets exhibit superior performance when evaluated on standard classification benchmarks, outperforming those pre-trained on classification tasks. Our findings indicate that depth assessment is a superior unsupervised pre-training method for enhancing the general capabilities of semantic segmentation models. To demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, we achieve an impressive 6.7% gain in mIoU on the KITTI validation set using our approach, surpassing state-of-the-art results. Moreover, models pre-trained on large-scale depth datasets exhibit a significant performance advantage over those pre-trained on classification tasks, as evidenced by an 8.2% gain in mIoU on the KITTI test set. Our project's source code, pre-trained models, and training scripts, have been made available. Furthermore, to evaluate the transferability of depth assessment, we also evaluate its effectiveness on other tasks, including instance segmentation and multi-class semantic segmentation. Our research shows that depth assessment can provide valuable knowledge to segmentation models, surpassing the performance of classification-based pre-training methods in various scenarios. As a result, depth assessment has become an attractive alternative to traditional pre-training methods. However, we also identify some limitations of depth assessment and discuss potential future research directions, including its unsuitability for tasks involving fine-grained classification due to its limited domain. Moreover, these traditional methods usually focus on specific genres, such as animation, making them less versatile. To overcome these limitations, we developed TCube, a novel video storytelling framework that uses a neural network to create engaging and coherent content from arbitrary starting points. TCube's ease of use allows it to be applied across various genres, and our results show that it outperforms existing solutions in both user preferences and video quality. With TCube, motion and other dynamic aspects are automatically generated, eliminating the need for manual setup and programming. Additionally, the network is capable of adapting to different styles and genres through simple input changes. Our research demonstrates that TCube's neural architecture produces high-quality content by analyzing the structure of the video through segmentation. This breakthrough enables the creation of new content in video storytelling, paving the way for more innovative applications in this field. Developers frequently come across unforeseen errors while programming, which hindrances their progress. To resolve these issues, they often visit stacks overflow, an online platform where developers share knowledge and experience through descriptive text, along with external links that point to relevant off-platform resources, such as video tutorials, programming tools, and data feeds. Despite their potential to enhance knowledge sharing, these external links are unexplored. To better understand the utility of these links, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the most shared external links on stacks overflow, focusing on how they evolve, their impact on knowledge sharing, and how they can be improved using a crowdsourcing technique that involves asking existing users to rate the usefulness of these links. Our findings show that while most links are useful, many are broken, redirect to stacks overflow questions, or contain irrelevant information. Our research proposes several improvements to the way knowledge is linked on stacks overflow, including updating links to point to permanent resources, using crowdsourced information to prioritize links, and organizing external links by tag, to boost their utility and effectiveness. In addition, our research highlights several areas for future research and development. Overall, our research demonstrates that crowds oursing can be employed to analyze and improve the quality of data feeds, such as stacks overflow's external links, to enhance software maintenance and evolution. Our research artifacts are available, including the crowdsourced data and the codes, at https://github.com/external-links-so. (From Preface to Paper)

Our understanding of the nature of dark matter, which can be seen through its gravitational effects, relies heavily on a complex issue known as the galaxy variability problem. Many potential solutions to this longstanding astrophysical issue have been presented in scientific publications. Unfortunately, due to a lack of consensus among these solutions and limited expertise in the relevant scientific literature, it has been difficult to comprehensively compare and evaluate them effectively. In an effort to better understand the galaxy variability problem, we conducted a thorough review of various solutions by analyzing both their strengths and weaknesses, focusing on key factors such as underlying assumptions, computational approaches, and the applied statistical methodology. Our goal is to promote transparency and reproducibility in the galaxy variability problem by identifying crucial aspects that have been overlooked in previous studies, as well as provide guidance on how future solutions can be compared fairly. Ultimately, our review aims to promote a collaborative approach to tackle the complex issue of galaxy variability. The source code used for this review is publicly available at https://github.com/pulipulit/galaxy-variability-solutions, and we intend for it to be a valuable resource for scientists in the field of galaxy research. The galaxy variability problem stems from apparent overdensities in dark matter halos observed in direct detection experiments, which need to be mitigated through solutions that account for systematic variations in detection sensitivity. By evaluating 23 solutions to this issue, our review aims to promote a collaborative approach to tackle the complex issue of galaxy variability. The review is now available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m1.fw-icomm.2022v1, and the associated source code can be found at https://github.com/pulipulit/galaxy-variability-solutions. Climate change is a pressing global issue that necessitates open communication among climate experts. However, the current state of climate information is fragmented, hindering effective communication among them. To address this problem, we have developed a climate information repository that seamlessly integrates relevant data from multiple sources. This knowledge repository powers a chatbot that provides climate experts with quick access to standardized climate information, enabling them to engage in informed discussions. Our approach demonstrates the significance of climate data repositories in facilitating expert dialogue and serves as a model for similar applications in related fields. Medical professionals need comprehensive information about a patient's symptoms, symptoms developments, and associated conditions to make accurate diagnoses and treatment decisions. Recent studies have employed natural language processing to extract symptom information from unstructured medical records. However, the majority of existing research has focused on a single hospital or institution, with limited transferability to other settings. To address this challenge, our paper aims to develop a model capable of accurately extracting symptoms and symptoms-related information in diverse medical centers. To achieve this, we assembled a dataset comprising three cardiovascular disease datasets from different hospitals. Our experiments revealed that fine-tuning a pre-trained model using hospital-specific data leads to poor generalizability across different hospitals. Instead, our proposed method incorporates pre-trained models and selectively oversamples patient information to improve the model's overall performance. When evaluated against three separate datasets, our method demonstrated superior performance, achieving a 24.57% increase in F1 score, and consistently outperforming other baseline models with consistent results across various hospital datasets. The code for our work is available on GitHub at https://github.com/jayie123/DGSE.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of quark stars consisting of spin-aligned (color octet) strange quarks under the influence of intense magnetic fields, employing the MIT bag model. Our thermal modeling incorporates both kinetic and magnetic contributions. We have developed a novel equation of state for the free energy density of spin-aligned quarks in the presence of a strong magnetic field, which demonstrates significant similarity to that of free fermions. Our findings reveal that as temperature increases, quark stars composed of spin-aligned quarks undergo thermal expansion. Furthermore, we computed the mass-radius relations of quark stars consisting of spin-aligned quarks across various magnetic field strengths and found that their radii exhibit a slight increase with magnetic field intensity. Our analysis also shows that these quark stars are more compact when they are hotter and have a stronger magnetic field. Additionally, we calculated the specific heat, speed of sound, adiabatic index, and skewness of pressure with respect to energy density, which display temperature-dependent behavior. Our study further reveals that as the magnetic field increases, these parameters demonstrate heightened temperature dependence. This research aims to contribute to advances in quark star physics and magnetic astrophysics, while also informing future studies of extreme astrophysical phenomena. Our proposed theoretical model of spin-aligned quark stars has the potential to improve our understanding of the structure and behavior of quark stars, which has been largely driven by the study of compact objects such as neutron stars and quark stars. Furthermore, this research is expected to yield valuable insights into the phenomenology of these quark stars, which has the potential to shed light on fundamental aspects of quark star physics. Our predicted results for the mass-radius and thermal profiles of quark stars are anticipated to be tested through the analysis of ultraluminous X-ray sources, as well as the study of other events involving intense compact objects. Finally, this research is expected to yield predictions for the behavior of quark stars that align with observational data, which will serve as a significant milestone in the advancement of quark star astrophysics. We address the issue of estimating nonlinear eigenvalues based on observations that are subject to noise. A one-dimensional estimation problem is solved using a minimization procedure that takes an L1 penalty to constrain the estimation, and further modifications are made to allow for the use of noisy spectral data. Both parametric and nonparametric cases are examined, and theoretical proofs of consistency and convergence rates are provided for all scenarios. Numerical experiments are conducted to demonstrate the performance of these methods. These experiments specifically investigate the use of nonlinear eigenvalue estimation in understanding brain function through fMRI, and reveal that the proposed techniques deliver accurate results in this application. Furthermore, a freely available R package called RNEV has been developed to facilitate the implementation of these methods. RNEV provides a range of features and functionalities that support the analysis of eigenvalue problems in various contexts. Details regarding the package, along with guidance on its usage, are available in an additional supplement to this paper. Additionally, the RNEV package is publicly available at the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/pesinju/RNEV. A brief tutorial on the usage of RNEV is also available at: https://pesinju.github.io/RNEV/index.html. Please note that the RNEV package is still under active development, and users are encouraged to submit feedback and suggestions for future enhancements. Key features and functionalities of RNEV, along with plans for its future development, are described in the provided supplement. We are committed to making RNEV a versatile and useful resource for the analysis of nonlinear eigenvalue problems. Keywords: Nonlinear eigenvalue problem, minimization with L1 penalty, consistency, convergence rate, adaptive estimation, interpolation, fMRI, brain function, RNEV package.

Furthermore, we show that they give rise to unique one-dimensional systems exhibiting ergodic behavior, along with certain recurrence patterns, applicable to any irrational, real number greater than one, regardless of its irrationality. We demonstrate that the flavor symmetry is shattered and flavor confinement occurs when the Chern-Simons constant is positive, resulting in the formation of scalar condensates. Unlike $\mathcal{N}=1$ SCFTs derived from $\mathcal{N}=2$ SCFTs, this flavor confinement does not arise from monopole operators. We derive energy bounds and spectrum constraints for the flavor theory, matching known properties of flavor theories with multiple monopole operators. Additionally, we propose an ansatz for the flavor theory Seiberg duality, where the flavor theory itself acts as a $\mathcal{N}=1$ SCFT. Furthermore, we explore the impact of dualities on confinement and the chiral phase diagram. An essential aspect of our research involves classifying and representing color and flavor cycles under $\mathrm{SO}(N_c)$, fostering a deeper understanding of the Chern-Simons gauge theory and flavor symmetry shattering/ confinement phases of gauge theories. Machine learning model interpretability is heavily dependent on feature importance, which can be misleading at times. This study introduces a novel visualization technique - Attribution Graph - to provide a more accurate interpretation of single and ensemble machine learning models. In contrast to traditional importance measures, Attribution Graphs showcase the contribution of each input feature to the predicted output based on the input's proximity to its optimal value, rather than its correlation with the output, thus offering a more nuanced understanding of how features contribute to the model's decision-making process. This research utilizes Attribution Graphs to offer insights into Random Forests, Gradient Boosting, and GBM-based deep learning models. To facilitate this analysis, a Python package - AGGraph - is also released, allowing users to easily create Attribution Graphs for their models. This package supports Random Forests, GBM, and XGBoost models, with plans to include support for LightGBM and GMBoost in future updates. Our findings reveal that while feature importance may suggest one feature is the most important, Attribution Graphs may indicate a different top contributor, highlighting their differing strengths and limitations. Moreover, Attribution Graphs can help reveal potential issues, such as overfitting, by detecting features with extreme skewness and/or zero values. This research also explores how Attribution Graphs can be utilized to detect issues in data, such as detecting features with extreme skewness and/or zero values, thus providing insights into Random Forests and GBM models. Federated Learning is an emerging technique for maintaining local data privacy, but training across multiple datasets is challenging due to differing dataset sizes and the interference they pose to each other when combined. Research has shown that mixing datasets randomly, a method called federated averaging, is not always optimal and can lead to subpar model performance. In an effort to address these issues, researchers have turned to trusted execution environments, which allow multiple datasets to train on a secure platform. This paper introduces Flatee, a secure federated learning framework utilizing Intel Software Guard Extensions that train multiple datasets on a secure platform. Flatee incorporates a new routine for securely combining gradients called Federated Quasi-Gaussian Mechanism, which adapts to the characteristics of training datasets to enhance model performance and security. Moreover, Flatee incorporates capabilities for securely updating model weights based on training iterations and provides two additional security features: partial results encryption and obfuscation of dataset statistics. Our experiments demonstrate that Flatee surpasses current Federated Learning frameworks in security and performance, while training models up to 10% better than traditional methods. Our evaluation also shows that the performance of Flatee surpasses conventional methods, reaching speeds of 49.88 cycles per millisecond for federated training. Moreover, the cryptographic operations integrated in the Trusted Execution Environment, such as scalar multiplication, reach speeds of 12.89 kilocycles per millisecond. Our source code is available at https://github.com/jupiretti/IntelSGE_FederatedLearning. A detailed description of the technical approach and results is available at https://arxiv.org/doi/10.48550/arXiv.2205.04133. With its integration of next-generation Trusted Execution Environments, Flatee represents a pioneering approach to maintaining user privacy and model performance in Federated Learning initiatives. It achieves this through its innovative combination of security features and efficiency optimizations, showcasing a new paradigm for Federated Learning training. Our findings indicate that Flatee outperforms current state-of-the-art Federated Learning frameworks in both security and performance, training models up to 10% better. Moreover, Flatee's source code is available at https://github.com/jupiretti/IntelSGE_FederatedLearning. A detailed description of our technical approach and results is available at https://arxiv.org/doi/10.48550/arXiv.2205.04133. With its utilization of cutting-edge Trusted Execution Environments, Flatee serves as a leading approach to maintaining privacy and performance in Federated Learning

Modern microservices applications consist of numerous, containerized processes communicating with each other through system calls. Traditional security frameworks focus on individual system calls, lacking consideration for real-world applications' complex call patterns. This work introduces a training-based approach for developing expressive system call policies, adaptable to diverse applications. Our system call policy learning method enables efficient policy creation, reducing the time and effort required to define a policy. This method also mitigates the risk of human-error induced policy breaches. The efficacy of this framework is demonstrated through our analysis of five open-source e-commerce applications, covering various scenarios. Furthermore, we show the security benefits of our system call policy learning method. Our evaluation reveals that, with minimal policy tuning, our method prevents malicious activity in the benchmark applications. For example, in our evaluation of a web service, our method prevented 97% of potentially harmful system calls. Our system call policy learning method is based on the Timeloops framework, allowing it to learn system call patterns within applications. This is achieved through the analysis of the applications' call sequences, prioritizing policy expressions that appear across multiple threads. Our evaluation demonstrates that our system call policy learning method is responsive, adapting to evolving applications. The learnability of our system call policy learning method is inversely related to the diversity of the applications' call patterns. Our system call policy learning method is designed to learn system call policies autonomously, but we also identify scenarios where manual policy guidance is beneficial. This is the case for applications requiring significant policy tuning or leveraging low-level system calls. Our analysis of the open-source benchmark applications is publicly available, allowing our system call policy learning method to be reproduced and evaluated. This includes application-specific call patterns, policy learning results, and system call counts. This data confirms our approach, offering new perspectives on learning system call policies. This could aid developers in applications we analyzed and others, potentially expanding the scope to other domains. The minor effects are negligible and can be disregarded for the purposes of this analysis. Focusing on the strong separation regime, where the orbital distances are significantly greater than the size of the black hole, we find that the Arrangements theorem does not apply as previously assumed. By developing new formulas based on the Arrangements theorem's framework, we provide a better understanding of the stellar orbital arrangements in this strong separation regime. These improved formulas take into account the Arrangements theorem's results and the effects of variable mass distributions. Additionally, we update the alpha parameter, which measures orbital anisotropy, to better accommodate variations in mass distributions. Our new findings are consistent with observations made by the Keck/LGS Adaptive Optics System. This paper introduces a cutting-edge approach called Random Model Predictive Control. It outlines a straightforward simulation method to generate random control inputs in advance, reducing online computation. The complexity of the algorithm is detailed, along with a comprehensive simulation demonstration that highlights its efficacy. Key performance metrics such as losses and standard deviations effectively evaluate the performance of the Random Model Predictive Control. By adjusting crucial parameters, optimal results are achieved, proving the versatility of the Random Model Predictive Control approach. Furthermore, theoretical analysis confirms the asymptotic convergence of the stochastic system to the desired target trajectory. In-depth mathematical proofs establish the validity of the approach, while a readily accessible mathematical formulation facilitates understanding and implementation. Ultimately, the Random Model Predictive Control approach presents a viable option for addressing the limitations of Model Predictive Control, particularly its high online computational demands. To showcase the Randolph Model Predictive Control, a dynamic system with input constraints was utilized, but the methodology is adaptable to a broad range of applications, potentially including Randolph-type systems with additional constraints. Key technical terms, including slidebar variables, are clearly defined for ease of comprehension. This paper bridges a gap in research by providing a comprehensive framework for feature representation through Independent Component Analysis (I CA) in the context of compressed sensing. From theoretical underpinnings to practical implementation, our methods and algorithms remain accessible to feature learning engineers. A fundamental contribution of our research is the development of a theoretical framework, comprising two main findings. Firstly, sparse signal recovery can be effectively represented through linear transformations. Secondly, feature extraction can be achieved by applying ICA to the compressed sensing coefficients. Building upon these findings, our study explores sparse sensing matrix properties, deriving both necessary and sufficient conditions for feature extraction. These conditions facilitate feature extraction in both synthetic and real-world scenarios. Our research demonstrates the feasibility of ICA on approximately sparse domains, exemplified through sparse pixel feature learning in image compression. Furthermore, our analysis reveals the potential for feature extraction using ICA even in the absence of sparse sensing matrices. An empirical evaluation of our methods was conducted across three datasets, showcasing state-of-the-art performance in classification tasks and comparable results for clustering. Notably, our feature maps extracted features in an approximate linear manner, as supported by the theoretical findings. Our source code is available at https://github.com/jbrenn2/compressible-ica. We are studying the properties of regions within the abelian quantum double model and their associated von Neumann algebras. Our previous research established that these regions form a hierarchical collection, and the algebras they comprise are part of a monoidal category. In this current work, we examine the interrelations between different sets of regional algebras within this collection. Our key finding is that these sets partition the space in a hierarchical manner, creating a category where the algebras are the objects and the morphisms are the inclusions between them. This category exhibits closedness under the tensor product, allowing us to expand the structure to a category of subalgebras within the quantum double model. In comparison, a similar structure has been found in the context of conformal quantum field theory, where it serves as a crucial element in the study of 2-dimensional surfaces. Building on these findings, we propose a new approach to studying the non-local structure of regions in quantum field theory. In a subsequent paper, we plan to apply this structure to study 2-dimensional bulk theories derived from regions. This pattern holds true up to local algebras, where the containing algebra contains no additional information beyond that found in its constituent parts. This work compiles one-loop triple-collinear splitting operators for color-sensitive and color-blind scenarios in dimensionally-regulated QCD, incorporating the convention where $d=3-\epsilon$ and expressing results in terms of a set of four universal operators. The derived expressions are formulated in terms of scalar integrals and are expressed with an explicit dependence on $\epsilon$. Additionally, this work provides a complete compilation of all relevant scalar integrals, facilitating the derivation of universal splitting kernels. The resulting expression for the triple-collinear splitting kernel $P_{qq}(z)$ is also presented in a form that is familiar in the soft-collinear effective theory. To verify the accuracy of our results, various checks have been performed. These checks include comparisons with available arithmetic expressions and with an independent calculation of the triple-collinear splitting kernel $P_{qq}(z)$. Furthermore, this work relates the ARZ evolution constants to a novel set of evolution constants based on the FCNC evolution constants, allowing for a re-interpretation of the ARZ constants in the context of dimensionless QCD. An important consequence of this re-interpretation is that it renders plausible the concept of "decoupling scales" $Q^2_\text{dec}$ in the context of dimensionless QCD. An alternative formula for the evolution constant $\Delta_{qq}^{(3)}$ is also provided, directly linked to the FCNC constant $\Delta_{\phi\phi}^{(2)}$. This work is supplemented by a public Mathematica code that computes the ARZ evolution constants based on the dimensionless QCD interpretation. This code also includes a supplementary section that details how the dimensionless QCD splitting kernels can be computed using the soft-collinear effective theory. Specifically, it details how to derive the dimensionless QCD kernel for the quark-mass term in the SCET, relevant at small values of $z$. This contribution is currently being submitted separately for publication. The Neron Desingularization, a complex algorithm spanning multiple decades, aims to give an intrinsic, canonical representation to a valuation ring's non-standard, extended polynomial ring. While the full ND algorithm is geared towards one-dimensional valuation rings, individual components have broad applications across all types of local rings. The Positive General Neron Desingularization, an optimized ND algorithm, leverages the concept of an order on an extended polynomial ring. This paper showcases a fully functional, automated PND implementation, capable of handling diverse, general one-dimensional local rings, and their associated valuation groups. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates the computational feasibility of PND through concrete examples and statistical analysis of runs on random input data. Additionally, the paper includes an appendix detailing a newly established relationship between PND and a related theorem, originally stated by Schapira and Saito, and later expanded upon by Alberge, Regnault, and Whitehouse. This relationship has further computational implications that are explored in the paper. The accompanying code, documented in a separate section, is freely accessible on GitHub at: <https://github.com/14m961/PND_jupyter_notebook>. A complementary package, also freely available at <https://github.com/14m961/pnd_python>, provides the necessary functionality to replicate the algorithm's computation. This package, incorporating the algorithm's concepts and methods, has been successfully tested in Python 3.x and 2.7.9 versions. Lastly, the accompanying IPython notebook, documented in the code section, showcases the algorithm's computation on an extensive array of well-known and randomly generated local rings. This collection of examples is also freely available at <https://github.com/14m961/pnd_data>. The library computes key intermediate results, enabling a deeper understanding of the PND algorithm's behavior, and has the potential to be developed into a general-purpose algorithm, and additionally, the library could be used as a testing suite for verifying the correctness of other PND implementations. The PND algorithm, having passed extensive statistical testing on random input data, appears to be a reliable and robust solution. This conclusion is further reinforced by analyzing how the algorithm's components interact, and by examining how well its results match the predictions based on the algorithm's parameter settings. A novel approach, which we refer to as'man-in-the-middle' (MitM), has emerged as a threat to these models: inserting unwanted elements into the protected data. Despite being debunked by scientific evidence, this conspiracy theory persists due to its combination of personal and economic interests. In multiple star systems, the interaction between component planets and other stars can lead to distinct orbital paths, ultimately resulting in various accretion rates across the system. This research focuses on predicting these accretion rates in hierarchical systems consisting of a pair of stars and a less massive companion, surrounded by a circumstellar disk. By applying the equilibrium approximation to the disk and modeling its response to the tidal interaction, we calculated the accretion rates of the primary and secondary stars under two scenarios: when the disk is affected by tidal interactions and when it is not. Our findings indicate that when the disk is affected, the primary star accretes more from the inner disk, while the secondary star accretes more from the outer disk. Conversely, when the disk is unaffected, the primary star primarily accretes from the inner disk, with minimal material coming from the outer disk. Additionally, when the disk is unaffected, the secondary star accretes more from the outer disk compared to when the disk is affected. Lastly, when the secondary star's mass equals or exceeds that of the primary, the primary star experiences heightened accretion rates across all scenarios. These predictions can help explain observed patterns of anomalous eccentricities among wide binary stars. Further, our models estimate that when the secondary star's mass equals or exceeds that of the primary, the primary star is expected to live up to 10% of its solitary existence life. Lastly, the critical distance at which the secondary star begins to significantly affect the primary's surroundings lies within the range of 30-60 times the primary star's radius. This research can help estimate the accretion rates of secondary stars in systems similar to those of wide binaries with late-type stars, such as Alpha Centauri A and B. Moreover, it is expected that the accretion rates of secondary stars in such systems will vary significantly, ultimately affecting their overall development. Ultimately, this phenomenon is anticipated to have a minimal impact on the primary stars' evolution, as their accretion rates are expected to remain relatively low, ultimately failing to halt or reverse their evolution. Conversely, the opposite is true for the secondary stars, as their accretion rates are expected to remain high enough to affect their overall development. Ultimately, this research is expected to lay the groundwork for accurate modeling of wide binary systems with late-type stars. We analyze the interaction between a moving atom and a slender mirror in a scan from far away to a point directly above the mirror's edge, using an approach that combines semi-analytical methods. When the atom passes this close to the mirror, its movement induces electromagnetic emissions. To calculate these emissions, we modify the Longitiudinal Finite-Difference Time-Domain (LFDTD) method, originally used for solving Maxwell's equations in static environments, to accommodate both moving charges and stationary boundaries. Our findings show that as the atom approaches the mirror, its movement generates two primary radiation patterns - a dipole and a quadrupole - which produce different emission spectra. Additionally, the atom can become excited by the electromagnetic interactions with the mirror, and its likelihood of excitation depends on its movement and its position above the mirror. This research provides new insights into the atom-mirror interactions and their impact on electromagnetic emissions, and demonstrates that the LFDTD method can accurately simulate these complex phenomena. Furthermore, our results show that the emitted radiation can take on non-threshold energies, and its patterns vary significantly according to the atom's movement and its proximity to the mirror. Most importantly, when the atom passes very close to the mirror, its movement induces electromagnetic emissions at frequencies significantly lower than its original emission frequencies, and its movement at these close distances can cause it to become excited, and this phenomenon occurs for distances as short as the atom's size. Lastly, the findings also emerge that for a neutrally moving atom passing above the mirror, its movement can induce electromagnetic emissions at frequencies lower than its original emission frequencies. This research leads to new understandings and predictions, and it opens up new avenues for experimentally verifying these predictions. Moreover, these results suggest the feasibility of using slender mirrors to induce electromagnetic emissions in atoms, and thereby expanding the range of frequencies that can be produced and manipulated in atomic emission spectra. Most importantly, this research demonstrates the ability of simulating complex atomic emissions using the LFDTD method, and successfully accounts for the effects of these emissions arising from moving charges interacting with stationary boundaries. This research introduces a multi-task model based on an adversarial network to enhance handwritten document images. The primary goal of this model is to improve the readability of degraded documents, but it also simultaneously performs text recognition as part of a self-supervised learning process. The primary adversarial network is trained to evaluate the clarity of the input image, contrasting it with real, clear images. The secondary recognition network is pre-trained on a standard dataset and leverages its internal stop-page and reduce-paddling mechanisms to adapt to the output format of the primary network, effectively utilizing discarded information. The model was tested on the DAWNBench dataset and demonstrated superior performance in restoring the readability of low-resolution, scanned documents. Notably, this model achieved outstanding results at a relatively low resolution of 16 pixels, with character accuracy rates surpassing state-of-the-art handwritten text recognition models even when operating at a higher resolution of 25 pixels. Moreover, this model successfully implemented transfer learning, reducing the impact of pre-trained models on handwritten text recognition while significantly enhancing the model's overall readability. The implementation code and associated training settings are available on the GitHub repository, enabling easy reproduction of the research findings. The model also shows great potential in handling diverse, in-domain scans and restoring the clarity of documents with severe degradation. Future work could build upon this model by incorporating page layout detection and adversarial training based on synthetic, clear documents. The research does have certain limitations: (1) The model is tailored to recognize text, but it may not perform as well on numbers and symbols; (2) The model relies on character-level output, which can make it prone to errors during recognition, especially when encountering longer sequences. Nonetheless, the model exhibits exceptional readibility while being relatively compact in size. Future research could focus on enhancing its adversarial training and transferring this knowledge to recognize numbers and symbols. Additionally, the model can be further refined to capture word or phrase-level information to supplement its recognition capabilities. The research does demonstrate that neural networks can be designed to capture the clarity of written information and utilize this clarity to enhance handwritten text recognition. The model also successfully reduced the impact of pre-trained models on handwritten text recognition while significantly enhancing the model's overall readibility. Moreover, the research does showcase that neural networks can be trained to transfer knowledge effectively and utilize transfer learning to maintain state-of-the-art performance even when operating at a low resolution and performing text recognition. The growth of Electronic Identity documents presents opportunities for enhanced security and system performance, but introduces challenges when legacy documents need to be converted to digital format. This paper outlines a solution for converting physical ID cards into digital format, leveraging Optical Character Recognition and machine learning-based techniques. As certain fields on Indonesian ID Cards are not legible by OCR, a further analysis using Natural Language Processing is implemented to extract the missing information. This leads to a 100% success rate in extracting all ID card fields. Our approach employs a dataset of 300, consisting of images of ID Cards and their corresponding specifications, created through a combination of Optical Character Recognition and human annotation. This dataset can also facilitate the analysis and validation of ID Card-related documents. This paper details our dataset, analysis method, and provides an open-source implementation for others to utilize. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance, extracting all ID card fields with 100% accuracy. This includes, but is not limited to, extracting the ID Card number, Name, Date of Birth, Place of Birth, and Address. This, in turn, enables the creation of a fully functional ID Card analyzer, enabling applications such as ID Card validation, name-based search, and date-of-birth-based search. Our ID Card analyzer boasts 97.97% accuracy in extracting ID Card fields, even when previously extracted fields are obscured. This makes our approach highly versatile and adaptable to diverse use cases. Moving forward, we intend to expand our capabilities to handle ID Cards with varied layouts and employ transfer learning to support ID Cards from other nations. Our ultimate goal is to create a leading, unbiased platform for ID Card analysis, empowering researchers and developers to contribute and benefit from a rich dataset of ID Cards. This, in turn, may facilitate ID Card-related research in fields such as Social Science and Law. Currently, we lack the necessary space to detail our future plans for natural language-based ID Card analysis. We hope this rich dataset will enable and further enrich researchers within these areas. To overcome these difficulties, this study develops a long short-term memory (LSTM) based channel estimation method. LSTM networks are particularly well-suited for modeling vehicular channel phenomena. Building on this idea, a resource-efficient scheme is devised to apply the LSTM network online, facilitating real-time use in practical applications. A comparative assessment is conducted to evaluate the performance of the proposed method against existing multi-path and deep learning based channel estimation techniques. The results show that the proposed method outperforms existing techniques, delivering improved normalized mean squared error (NMSE) performance and faster convergence rates. Moreover, the LSTM network's ability to learn and adapt to changing environments is demonstrated. Follow-on work could focus on leveraging LSTM networks for purposes beyond channel estimation. Additionally, the IEEE 802.11p standard is explored as a potential basis for vehicular communication systems. The IEEE 802.11p system operates in the 5.9 GHz frequency band and is heavily influenced by multi-path and fast fading phenomena. A thorough analysis is undertaken to assess the suitability of IEEE 802.11p for vehicular applications and to gather data for training the LSTM network. The study's findings are expected to contribute to the development of efficient channel estimation methods for IEEE 802.11p and other similar vehicular systems. A comparable dataset, collected using two vehicles equipped with USFDA compliant IEEE 802.11p transceivers, is made publicly available.
