We introduce a novel approach to neural network design that automates the process of adding new nodes and connections based on data, eliminating the need for iterative training. Unlike traditional methods, our approach identifies the optimal network configuration directly. Building on the principles of the Cramer-Rao theorem, we develop a unbiased estimator of the conditional probability distribution of the data given the model parameters. This innovative method requires no gradient information, instead using the likelihood of the data given the model to generate an optimization landscape. Our results demonstrate that the temporary surrogates' convergence is sufficient for achieving an acceptable level of likelihood. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach by comparing it to traditional neural networks on popular regression and classification datasets. Our findings show that our method consistently produces lower generalisation errors and achieves convergence an order of magnitude faster than iterative training methods. Our approach has the added benefit of producing interpretable results in the form of marginal probability distributions of the data given the model parameters. Due to its high computational requirements, our approach is currently only suitable for use with small datasets. Our work marks the first application of the principles of the Cramer-Rao theorem to the design of neural networks. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/pesimista/grfnn. Our approach is inspired by the idea of using probability theory to design neural networks, an idea initially proposed by Fisher more than nine decades ago. Our findings demonstrate that our approach, though simplistic in form, is a robust foundation for neural network design. Our research contributes to the long-standing debate on the design of neural networks, offering a probability-theoretic alternative to other approaches. Our work may also contribute to the design of other machine learning models through the application of the principles of the Cramer-Rao theorem. Our approach, though not the most efficient in terms of computational requirements, marks an important milestone in the design of neural networks using probability theory and offers a positive answer to the question of whether it is possible to design neural networks through the application of the principles of the Cramer-Rao theorem. Our research opens up the possibility of exploring other probability-theoretic designs of neural networks, as demonstrated by the comparison of our approach with other probability-theoretic designs, such as the Gaussian process, which we leave for future research to formalise and prove. The task of relation extraction aims to extract meaningful relationships between entities from natural language text. Conventional approaches to this task rely heavily on mark-up language, but with the advent of neural networks, researchers have explored the potential of phrasal-level representation for relation extraction. However, training models in this framework often necessitates extensive labeled data, of which there is a scarcity. To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel framework that integrates knowledge graph link prediction to guide model training for relation extraction. Our method leverages the vast amount of unlabelled data and the existing knowledge graph to determine unsolved relationships, thereby enhancing model performance without requiring more labelled data. Experimental evaluations on four benchmarks reveal consistent improvements in our method's efficacy. Furthermore, our study demonstrates that the proposed framework's results surpass those of prominent state-of-the-art baselines. To facilitate replication, our code, data, and pre-trained models are available on GitHub at https://github.com/HotPotATM/ER-KGLP. A demo of our model's capability can be accessed via http://er.demos.talpalin.org. Extensive model predictions are hosted online at https://er.predict.talpalin.org. To support the development of this framework in commercial applications, our knowledge graph dataset is available at https://kg.datasets.talpalin.org. This dataset also serves as a knowledge graph extension tool, allowing users to expand their existing knowledge graphs with high accuracy. Our research is made possible by the support of AI Seed, a leading AI research and development program. More information about AI Seed is available at https://www.aiseed.tech. Knowledge graph link prediction, a capability of which can be seen in action at http://lpp.demos.talpalin.org, and which was made possible by our knowledge graph dataset at https://lpp.datasets.talpalin.org, has also been shown to have numerous other applications, including but not limited to enhancing the accuracy of question answering by predicting additional knowledge graph entities, and broadening context words' definitions by predicting related entities in the knowledge graph. In a a N+1 = (3+1)) dimensional QCD plasma with anisotropic momentum, we calculate the fragmentation characteristics of a heavy quark-antiquark pair in the direction of the longest momentum axis. Our analysis accounts for both real and virtual quark-antiquark pairs, utilizing a quasi-particle Debye mass framework and incorporating finite baryonic chemical potential. A numerical evaluation of this quark-antiquark potential reveals that, in the presence of anisotropy, quark-antiquark binding is decreased, resulting in a lower quark-antiquark mass than in an isotropic environment. Additionally, the quark-antiquark fragmentation in the direction of the shortest momentum axis becomes less favored as anisotropy increases. For small values of anisotropy, quark-antiquark binding is decreased by the presence of baryonic chemical potential, resulting in a lower quark-antiquark mass than in zero baryonic chemical potential. However, at higher anisotropy, baryonic chemical potential has the counterintuitive effect of increasing the quark-antiquark binding, resulting in a higher quark-antiquark mass than in zero baryonic chemical potential. A summary of quark-antiquark binding behavior in various environments is provided. Quark-antiquark binding is decreased by anisotropy, lowered quark mass, presence of baryonic chemical potential (unless accompanied by anisotropy), temperature, volume, and number of space dimensions. Finally, quark-antiquark binding becomes less favored as it becomes more distant, Fock-Hahn, rather than bound, quark-antiquark pairs in the hot QCD environment. We seek a universal method to encode fixed-length input sequences into a fixed-length output vector while maintaining segment-level detail. Current predictive models, including T5 and CoT5, fall short in retaining order information within their output representations. In real-world applications, training machine learning models with labeled data is often impractical or unobtainable. This issue is compounded by datasets experiencing shifts in their underlying distributions as time progresses or when dealing with diverse populations. This study addresses the challenge of adapting ML models to accommodate these changes by redefining the problem as a causal inference task. Specifically, we reinterpret source domain labels as the result of these underlying distributions and aim to learn a transformation that can predict both the original label and the cause of these shifts in the target domain, utilizing unlabelled target domain data. This novel framework is built upon the foundation of causal effect modeling and is implemented through the development of a semi-generative model, which integrates the principles of graphical models and generative adversarial networks. Our proposed approach is shown to outperform state-of-the-art methods in handling dataset shifts and maintaining label consistency, as evidenced by comprehensive experiments across multiple domains. The ability of neural networks to learn precise predictions is heavily dependent on their architecture and the nature of their weights. Real-valued weights restrict neural networks from fully capturing the inherent properties of certain problems, such as the sign structure of wavefunctions in quantum chemistry, due to the inherent nature of real numbers. This limitation gives rise to the sign dilemma, a significant challenge in quantization. Our research highlights the potential of complex-valued weights to resolve this issue. By transforming real-valued networks into complex-valued ones, we demonstrate that the sign dilemma can be overcome. This breakthrough has far-reaching implications, enabling the use of low-precision complex-valued networks for quantum chemistry applications. Moreover, we show that the optimal parameter distribution for complex-valued weights resembles a specific pattern and derive a reliable approximation for this distribution. Furthermore, we develop an effective method to generate such parameter distributions dynamically during training. Our results reveal a substantial reduction in precision requirements for networks with complex-valued weights, exemplified by a 3.5 times decrease in binary weight magnitude for a small chemistry benchmark. This finding indicates that complex-valued networks offer a promising solution to the sign dilemma, thus opening up new avenues for chemistry applications at low precision. Recent research has focused on the reliability of machine learning models against malicious attacks. In this study, we expand on existing research by introducing a new requirement - that the model's predictions must be accurate not just for any given attack, but specifically for attacks that can be anticipated and verified. To meet this challenge, we develop a framework that combines traditional Bayesian learning with concepts from theoretical cryptography. This innovative approach results in a robust Bayesian classifier, one that achieves a 0-1 loss function landau symbol big O of sqrt(n) with high probability, where n represents the number of samples used in training. Through comprehensive evaluation of real-world image classification datasets, we demonstrate the efficacy of our model in withstanding sophisticated attacks while maintaining superior accuracy and verifiable security. Importantly, our robust Bayesian classifier is capable of ascertaining whether an encountered attack can be deflected, thereby precluding costly and potentially harmful consequences. This unique ability sets our model apart from current solutions. Furthermore, our analysis underscores the inherent trade-offs between predictive accuracy, security, and verifiability. This pioneering work brings adversarial robustness into the realm of formal verification, marking the first instance to our knowledge. With ongoing advancements in deep learning techniques, our methodology can be adapted to accommodate increasingly complex models. With high confidence, our model will serve as a solid foundation for future developments in reliable machine learning. Each step involves constructing a renormalized Hamiltonian through a consistent Taylor series expansion of the original interaction with respect to electron-boson coupling strength. We demonstrate the convergence of this series and its implications on sum rules related to parquet theory. We also propose a practical approach to iterate the Taylor series and suggest a useful strategy for simplifying the resulting expressions by eliminating redundant terms. We then apply this methodology to construct a Hamiltonian that models a Hubbard model with nearby nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor interactions. To tackle the associated non-trivial sign problem, we outline a method to compute all parquet diagrams related to the model's particle-hole channel. We verify the correctness of our approach by successfully computing a sum rule associated with the particle-hole channel. Furthermore, we showcase the application of our methodology in a simulation involving a finite 6x6 lattice of electrons. We then extend the method to the more general case of fermions with n-component spinor characteristics, where n can be any number greater than or equal to four. However, we note that for values of n beyond four, the associated series expansions become infinite due to a lack of sufficient constraints on electron-boson coupling strength. To address this issue, we outline a random phase approximation (RPA) that can be used to iteratively improve the renormalized Hamiltonian in increments of four. We propose several possible strategies for applying the RPA in a meaningful way. Through this work, we aim to revive and reinterpret parquet theory in a more predictive framework. In particular, we show that polarization operators related to the renormalized Hamiltonian can be computed efficiently using a finite number of diagrams. This study assesses the changes in data complexity of Western music from the late 19th to the early 21st centuries. Comparing recordings from the late 19th and early 20th centuries with more recent data, findings reveal a shift towards lower data complexity. Within the last century, changes in data complexity are minimal, suggesting that the impact of electronic media on sound characteristics has reached a plateau. As data complexity stabilizes, differences between music periods from different cities diminish, implying a new era of musical homogeneity. These observations are consistent with social theories of globalization and the converging nature of music styles in popular culture. One potential explanation for these findings lies in the widespread adoption of standardized recording technologies and the internet, facilitating global access to a vast collection of musical styles. The reduced diversity of sound characteristics in modern music may be seen as a symbol of cultural capitalism, where diversity becomes a commodity that can be bought and sold. To summarize, this study offers a novel perspective on music evolution based on data complexity, leveraging digital audio analysis to quantify changes in sound characteristics over time. The significant shift towards more stable data complexity since the early 20th century can be viewed through the lens of social theory, from cultural imperialism to global connectivity. The implicit equivalence between sound characteristics and cultural diversity raises important ethical considerations for the music industry, where the commercialization of diversity becomes a fundamental value. The digital transformation of music analysis has far-reaching implications, empowering researchers to monitor cultural evolution digital footprints. The increasing emphasis on computer science education's 'computational thinking' and'reproducible research' emphasizes the importance of aesthetically pleasing and interactive code, particularly for educational purposes. A growing body of research highlights the positive impact of computational creativity and interactive visualizations in promoting engagement and collaboration. Our research explores the potential of 'computational playfulness,' a concept that shares parallels with Abraham Maslow's 'hierarchy of needs' - fulfilling basic functional needs, meeting interactive requirements, and ultimately satisfying the higher-level emotional needs of users. To investigate this concept, we designed and implemented a 'computer science beauty' contest, evaluating 1,234 publicly accessible GitHub repositories of educational projects based on 12 criteria from aesthetics to usability. Our analysis reveals that while most projects focus on fulfilling 'performance' and 'usability' needs, few meet the 'computational playfulness' need by incorporating features such as interactive visualizations and a clear project demo. These findings suggest that educational projects, particularly those related to reproducible research, significantly fall short of meeting this need for playfulness. Our study also identifies GitHub's'stars' as a reliable indicator of a project's aesthetic and interactive qualities, and suggests various strategies to enhance computational playfulness in existing projects, including the incorporation of interactive visualizations, detailed documentation, and social sharing options. To promote computational playfulness in computer science education, we propose establishing a repository of 'beautiful' projects, along with a package manager that allows users to easily incorporate these projects into their own repositories. This study paves the way for future research into the relationship between computational creativity and the quality of interactive code, and provides guidelines for evaluating and improving the aesthetic and interactive qualities of reproducible research projects. In addition, we make available a comprehensive dataset of evaluated GitHub projects, along with the code and evaluation protocols used to support this research. This dataset serves as a seed for a computational repository of aesthetically pleasing projects, and can be utilized by computer scientists to study the relationship between code quality and aesthetic qualities. Similarly, it can also be used by educators to select attractive projects for teaching purposes, and by developers to evaluate and improve the aesthetic and interactive qualities of their own projects. Furthermore, we make available the code and evaluation protocols of this research at: https://danielfranco.github.io/harmony-in-ghaesthetics/. A cutting-edge technique known as Standardized Enhanced Inference Network addresses a critical challenge in making predictions based on incomplete data, particularly in the field of deep learning. This approach combines a prediction model with a modeling component that estimates probabilities for missing data input into the prediction model, leading to improved accuracy and enhanced interpretability. To address these limitations, we introduce a modified standard enhancement method. First, we replace the mean probability output with the median, retaining more information. Second, we standardize the uncertainty distribution using z-scores instead of probabilities, allowing for flexible uncertainty representations. Third, we employ a neural network to model the uncertainty distribution directly, resulting in improved accuracy and interpretability over the mean probability output. This research targets the uncommon out-of-domain challenge in conversational AI, where a model is tasked with recognizing phrases beyond its training data when encountered in real-world dialogue with users. To achieve better ood detection, we introduce a new approach, the Mixture of Experts for Out-of-Domain, which utilizes a pair of classification networks to distinguish between the two types of out-of-domain phrases. Our experiments using the Twitter ood dataset demonstrate that this method enhances ood detection performance when employed in conjunction with existing pre-trained models. The resulting framework, called unilateral resynchronizability, is more general than its traditional counterpart. A straightforward algorithm is proposed to determine, in linear time, whether a term-generating machine can be transformed into a resynchronizable one and, if so, to implement this transformation. The study further explores the theoretical aspects of unilateral resynchronizability by establishing its key properties and proving that verifying resynchronizability remains a complex problem despite the linear-time verification of bilateral resynchronizability. Additionally, the study investigates the trade-offs between different implementations of unilateral resynchronizability and offers a prototype for practical use. Moreover, the study provides examples of real-world applications where resynchronizability can be useful. Finally, the study extends the concept of resynchronizability to its probabilistic counterpart. In the context of combinatorial mathematics, generalized convolutions hold significance across various fields. They find practical application in problems involving divisors and their multiples, clump detection within astronomical images, and more. Due to the high computational demands of certain generalized convolutions, a brute force approach proves unfeasible for larger inputs. This present work aims to mitigate this limitation by introducing an innovative method to compute generalized convolutions efficiently. Building upon prior research by G. Nemes that established a novel relationship between generalized convolutions and the partition function, we develop an efficient algorithm to calculate these convolutions. This algorithm initially computes the partition function using the approach outlined in R. HonsBauer's research, then efficiently calculates the desired generalized convolution through division. We validate our method through extensive examples and comparative analysis with the brute force approach. Furthermore, we make available a computational package, known as convolve_generalized, that enables seamless execution of our algorithm in Mathematica. Additionally, we present an open-source version of this package, referred to as convolve_generalized, for efficient use in astronomical image processing applications through clump identification and other analytical services. Lastly, we make available a dataset, available through DOI 10.17632/5z9b2789x5, that includes the results of the convolve_generalized function for all pairs of $n,\ell\le 40$ as computed by the provided method. This dataset serves as a valuable resource, saving others the effort of computing these values, while also verifying the correctness of our approach with notable findings. The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995, initially classified as an ultra-cool brown dwarf, sparked significant debate among astronomers. Recent high-provability spectra of this object, obtained through AO-conjugated techniques, have led to speculations about GJ 229B's nature. Analyzing these spectra with advanced algorithms capable of accurately extracting spectral features even from noisy data, has prompted a re-examination of the object's nature. Our studies, based on synthetic spectra models of atmospheric compositions, suggest that GJ 229B's atmosphere is characterized by strong C2 and CH4 absorption, thus making it unlikely to be a late-T dwarf. Instead, we propose that GJ 229B's atmosphere must be extremely humid to explain its observed spectral features. These findings resolve the long-standing enigma surrounding GJ 229B by ruling out the Brown-dwarf hypothesis, instead pointing towards the object being a giant planet with a highly humid atmosphere. This planetary solution is consistent with the object's expected contraction into a low-mass giant planet within the next 2.6 billion years. Moreover, our studies reveal that GJ 229B's highly humid atmosphere is a long-lived trait, extending to the object's evolution as a giant planet. The object's highly unusual retrograde orbit also supports its planetary origin, with its highly eccentric evolution a potential result of past dynamical interactions. A fundamental aspect of a market's functioning, beyond simply matching buyers and sellers, lies in ensuring that transactions are genuine and reflect actual intentions.  This concept is known as double faces, a phenomenon first identified in the 1960s by economists.  In this study, we demonstrate that a specific type of market mechanism, the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves auction, is capable of detecting and preventing instances of double facing.  Furthermore, we show that any market mechanism capable of matching buyers and sellers must either be vulnerable to double facing or reveal a participant's private valuation assessment, a notion known as preference preference preservation.  While the VCG mechanism may appear to introduce an unnecessary surplus of goods or services due to its tendency to induce overbidding, we find that this phenomenon is actually an inherent consequence of the market designer's information constraints, rather than a flaw in the mechanism itself.  Ultimately, we propose a new approach to double facing that takes into account the distinct roles of market designers and producers, highlighting the need for further research in this area.  Additionally, we outline potential areas for future exploration, such as the development of standardized contracts and the investigation of specific types of double facing.  In contrast to existing literature, which has focused largely on the effects of double facing on market designers, we argue that the double facing problem is one that should be addressed by the market designer.  We explore the challenges and opportunities presented by different types of double facing, as well as the resulting paradox of when it is beneficial for it to occur.  Finally, we propose a framework for double facing in the context of a supply curve, revealing certain inherent limitations of market mechanisms.  Ultimately, we conclude that the double facing problem is a complex and multifaceted challenge.  Additional research is needed to fully grasp its implications. A curve in the plane is called n-nonexpansive if it induces the same topology on the plane divided into n equal sectors, and 1-expansive if the opposite holds. We demonstrate that any curve which is not 1-nonexpansive can be decomposed into finitely many cyclic components, and show that this property distinguishes the class of nonexpansive curves from other curves. Additionally, we construct compact manifolds whose boundary is comprised of a nonexpansive curve, and resolve a prior problem concerning the equivalence of 2- and 3-nonexpansive curves. Finally, we define a type of curve, and its associated map, for which the moduli space has a finite covering degree. These constructions rely on a method of "cyclic decomposition" which may be of separate interest. Our work is motivated by a combination of prior research, and new questions and problems are posed within. Specifically, we investigate the relationship between the class of nonexpansive curves and that of quasi-Finsler metrics, as well as the regularity of nonexpansive curves. Furthermore, we consider the generalization of these results to higher dimensions. Following the advice of Misha Gromov, we have attempted to make the introduction and text highly accessible, and hope that these results will prove of interest to a broad audience. The chess community's self-organizing structure, particularly the classification of chess openings, demonstrates human information systems' ability to manage informational overload. By analyzing data from the chess.com platform, this research investigates the intricacy and similarity of chess openings. The study examines the hierarchical organization of chess openings from multiple perspectives and evaluates the effectiveness of different distance metrics to cluster these concepts together. The results reveal a complex, nested pattern to the chess openings, with the most challenging ones to master located at the core. The research identifies distinct groups within the periphery, comprising openings that are either strategically weak or tactically demanding. Additionally, the analysis highlights similarities between chess players in their favorite openings and the evolution of these experts' favorite moves over time. The findings provide insights for both chess players and artificial intelligence developers to optimize their approaches to the game. By simulating stellar mergers, we determine the final configuration of the resulting massive star. Our findings indicate that supernova explosions occur at advanced stages of stellar evolution. Pulsar rotation periods are dictated by the angular momentum conservation during the merger process, while their magnetic fields are influenced by the particle-accretion process post-merger. Our model yields a plausible density distribution of millisecond pulsars, aligning with observed data, and provides insight into pulsar magnetospheres. Furthermore, our research enables calculation of heavy-element abundance in the light of observed asymptotic giant branch pulsar parameters. Our stellar-evolution model allows for the computation of supernova explosion energies, which in turn affects gamma-ray burst events. Ultimately, our analysis reveals that supernova explosions are primordial events, occurring early in stellar evolution, whereas neutron stars form and undergo AIC processes at later stages. Our findings will contribute to the development of more accurate microphysical pulsar models, thereby enhancing the overall understanding of these celestial entities. Moreover, our research has implications for the study of compact star doubletons, compact stars with distinct masses, and may shed light on the occurrence of giant pulses emanating from celestial sources. Our work remains susceptible to modification, and we anticipate that future updates will originate from the realm of stellar physics, which might yield additional criteria to construct celestial models. To address these questions, we present a new approach called MemoNav, which is a detailed reinforcement learning framework designed to select memory insertion points and navigate using path-based recall strategies. Unlike existing methods, MemoNav focuses on exploration, thereby discovering novel navigation techniques. Through evaluations of MemoNav on two challenging navigation datasets, we observe significant performance gains compared to state-of-the-art models. Specifically, MemoNav achieves 10-20% higher success rates and 10-30% faster navigation speeds than existing models. Notably, MemoNav's multi-path recall strategy allows it to adapt to changing situations and demonstrate robustness in the field. Through analyses of MemoNav's behaviors, we identify key factors that influence recall strategies and demonstrate the potential of navigation through recall. Our code is available at https://github.com/rustyruby/MemoNav.

A vertex $v$ in a graph $G$ is considered a metric source if the positions of every other vertex can be determined by the distances to $v$. The minimum number of vertices required to act as metric sources in a graph is called its metric dimension, or $md(G)$ when referring to a specific graph. A generalized version of this concept, called $k$-metric dimension, or $k$-md, involves finding the minimum number of vertices needed such that at least $k$ distances between pairs of vertices can be uniquely determined. We explore the $k$-md property in several types of graphs, including infinite paths, cycles of specific lengths, and squares of these graphs. We then look at the specific case of trees, or graph structures, and establish a connection between their diameter and metric dimension. Ultimately, we investigate the computational complexity of determining whether a given graph has a particular $k$-md value. We then present a simplified approach to finding metric dimensions in certain graph configurations. We also establish relationships between different $k$-md values for the same graph. We also look at another generalized version of the concept, called $\Delta$-metric dimension, or $\Delta$-md, in which a vertex $v$ in graph $G$ is considered a metric source if it has a unique distance to every other vertex with a maximum distance $\Delta$ to $v$. Machine learning algorithms are often applied to systems with clear answers but uncertain premises, leading to a limited understanding of their confidence levels. In contrast, Argument-Based Reasoning systems, such as those used in logic and verification, naturally incorporate degrees of uncertainty associated with arguments. However, current methods for handling ambiguity in these systems are largely ad-hoc. In response, we introduce the concept of Indecision Forests, a general framework for learning under quantified ambiguity in Argument-Based Reasoning systems. By combining techniques from both machine learning and logic, Indecision Forests allow a portion of the system to remain undecided, as represented by the state of knowledge, while drawing conclusions based on the best available arguments. Through case studies involving both a simplified example and a more complex system from program verification, we demonstrate that Indecision Forests can yield precise results and outperform existing methods for handling ambiguity. In particular, we find that Indecision Forests can reveal previously hidden assumptions underlying the original system and even facilitate analysis of systems with inherent contradictions. As such, Indecision Forests offer a valuable tool for understanding and improving the argumentative foundations of machine learning models. In the future, we intend to expand Indecision Forests to accommodate learning from examples. In addition, we plan to apply Indecision Forests to a wider range of systems, including those in knowledge graph and document analysis. It is also our hope that Indecision Forests can shed new light on the foundations of deep learning. In particular, Indecision Forests could be used to study the effect of quantified uncertainty on the robustness of machine learning models. In addition, Indecision Forests may provide insights into the role of assumptions in the validation of self-driving cars. In general, Indecision Forests offer a new paradigm for machine learning that integrates the concepts of knowledge, arguments, and uncertainty from logic. In this integration, Indecision Forests go beyond existing models of machine learning, which typically ignore these issues. In the long term, we aim to make Indecision Forests available as a Python package. In the short term, we intend to apply Indecision Forests to systems for explaining reasons in counterfactual reasoning and for translating arguments in multi-agent systems. Conventional evaluation in software testing education relies on thoroughness. This study examines whether inquiry-based conceptual answers can serve as a more effective evaluation method. An empirical investigation was conducted, involving two groups of students, one answering conceptual questions and the other answering detailed questions. The levels of concept, process, and tool understanding were assessed in both groups. The results showed that, although there were differences between the groups, both levels of understanding were achieved. This indicates that, while not replacing traditional evaluation entirely, inquiry-based conceptual questions can offer an additional means of assessing students' conceptual skills within software testing education.

Despite the popularity of Graph Convolutional Networks, a comprehensive understanding of their generalization performance remains lacking. In this study, we establish the generalization effectiveness of Graph Convolutional Networks through manageable theoretical analysis. Our theoretical framework accounts for diverse types of graph convolutional layers and nonlinear functions. Our results reveal that the graph convolutional layer integrates information from the graph, and that the nonlinear function combines this information. Furthermore, we prove that the combination of graph convolutional and nonlinear layers constitutes an over-blurring effect, as found in traditional convolutional networks. Our theoretical findings are supported by polyhedral geometry and proxy loss analysis. Our experiments demonstrate that the design of Graph Convolutional Networks resembles that of traditional convolutional networks. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/nsercpd/GBN-over-blurring.

Analyzing the spectral characteristics of these objects required re-evaluating the galaxy cluster's thermal plasma emission, as the existing models were insufficient. Our research introduces a new model for the intracluster medium, PEARLS, designed to accurately reproduce the observed spectra. This model utilizes a density profile with radial discontinuities and non-spatially uniform cooling regions. Utilizing PEARLS, we successfully deconvolved the spectra of the two objects, revealing the presence of two stellar populations: a red giant and a red dwarf. This analysis also validated the presence of a massive ($\sim 4.5\times 10^{14}$ $M_{\odot}$) CCN3 galaxy, detected by JWST, which is less luminous than previously thought. This study demonstrates that JWST can utilize the spectral continuum to identify early-type stars at cosmological distances. The relationship between quantum states and physical observables is the foundational insight of quantum theory. However, certain generalized theories of quantum physics, such as those incorporating unnormalizable "distributions" as primary mathematical objects, complicate this dynamic. To address these variations, we develop a unified mathematical framework by establishing a precise mathematical equivalence between these approaches to quantum theory. Specifically, we show that the two perspectives are connected through a formal mathematical relationship called a categorical adjunction. By exploring this adjacency, we identify the underlying mathematical structure of quantum theory that remains consistent across all variations of the theory. Our findings are further illustrated by examining the boundedness of the fractional shift operator when applied to functions within $H^p(\mathbb{Z})$, as well as its invertibility and essential spectrum under varying $p$ values. Lastly, we delve into the fractional counter-part of Riesz systems within $H^p(\mathbb{Z})$, with $1 < p < \infty$. The investigation includes the determination of necessary and sufficient conditions for the boundedness of fractional shift operators when applied to functions within $H^p(\mathbb{Z})$, as well as the characterization of essential spectra of fractional shift operators. Our analysis also provides a generalized version of Lutz's theorem. Our study tests the robustness of this concept of stability through a double-blind online auction experiment where human bidders compete in a second-price bidding scenario with variable payments. We assess the reliability of this concept by comparing it to traditional biddable outcomes and explore its potential as a payment mechanism for a wide range of auctions. Our results show that the concept of stability is not universally accepted by human bidders as the most preferred payment method, but it does score higher than the traditional biddable outcome option. Additionally, bidders' reservations are analyzed through a stated preference survey, revealing a preference for stability among bidders who win auctions, but not among those who lose. However, non-winning bidders show a preference for a biddable outcome over stability, likely due to a loss aversion phenomenon. In summary, we conclude that while stability has its advantages, it is not universally trusted by human bidders as a payment method. Furthermore, we observe that the payment method affects winners' welfare, demonstrating a potential shortcoming of stability in real-world auction design. Compared to similar models trained with the complete rs-fMRI data, this breakthrough indicates that targeting key brain regions can significantly improve ADHD diagnosis.  Furthermore, data augmentation was employed to increase the diversity of available data, resulting in improved diagnostic outcomes. The novel approach of identifying critical regions and data augmentation proves to be valuable tools in machine learning-based diagnosis of ADHD. In our investigation, we explore an epidemic SISI model where individuals interact and spread diseases in distinct time periods. This model is based on an underlying network whose connectivity evolves over time according to predetermined cycles. We define an epidemic in this context as events that occur when the size of the infected population exceeds a certain threshold in any given time period. We analyze the probabilistic aspects of these epidemics and derive an expression for the probability of an epidemic occurring within a specific time frame, given that the population is initially composed of infected and uninfected individuals. This expression further generalizes to the case where the infected population is comprised of multiple groups. We also investigate the particular case where the population is equally divided between infected and uninfected individuals, deriving an expression for the probability of an epidemic that matches a prior result from Szabó, et al., primarily due to the equalization of certain probabilities in this scenario. Our approach for handling this problem involved the use of generating functions. Our findings for this distinct-time epidemic model contrast those typically obtained through continuous-time epidemic models. Ultimately, the significance of our investigation into this distinct-time epidemic model lies in its potential application to understanding real-world phenomena such as the spread of diseases among populations with irregular schedules of daily interactions. Additionally, our study may be relevant to modeling social behavior among individuals with distinct active and inactive periods. This includes examples such as students attending school and those working non-school hours. An interesting extension to our study would involve incorporating disease recovery into the epidemic model. However, due to the limited scope of our investigation, this potential extension is left as a possibility for future research. Our computation methods are equally applicable to scenarios where the infected population is comprised of multiple distinct groups. Therefore, our study should not be limited to scenarios of equal infection and un-infection probabilities. Rather, our findings are intended to be broadly interpretable in scenarios where the population is initially composed of infected and uninfected individuals in any proportion. A new category of topological invariant, capable of describing nodal surfaces in momentum space, has been explored. This review begins with a theoretical foundation and then examines recent developments in photonic systems, where engineers design structures to produce topological nodal surfaces. Research has also been conducted using ultracold atoms, as well as in studies of Dirac/Weyl points in optical systems. Novel techniques for creating topological nodal surfaces through optical manipulation are also discussed. This includes both passive designs and the use of optical vortices, which enable the creation of topological nodal lines. This area of study is an active and dynamic field, and this review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of the field's theory and recent applications. In oscillatory systems driven by a pacemaker, intrinsic dynamics is supplemented by an external influence that initiates and regulates a specific type of wave propagation. This wave, present in several biological settings such as heart cells and skeletal muscle, is influenced by two key factors: action potential generated by the pacemaker and the relaxation of the tissue following the impulse. We have developed analytical methods to estimate the speed of this wave in two distinct scenarios, one where tissue relaxation is instantaneous and another where relaxation occurs gradually. Our analysis involves examining the effects of spatially non-uniform pacemaker activity and tissue characteristics on wave velocity. Additionally, we have performed numerical simulations to verify our analytical findings and observed that under certain conditions, even a minor disparity in pacemaker activity among cells can still result in coherent rhythmic activity. Our study's conclusions are also applicable to other types of waves governed by oscillatory systems. Ultimately, we hope that our analysis will help inform ongoing research into the spatiotemporal dynamics of generated waves. We have developed two distinct algorithms for estimating the von Neumann entropy of a quantum state $\rho$. The first algorithm employs a variation of the quantum principle component analysis (QPCA) method to obtain an approximate maximum likelihood estimation of $\rho$. The likelihood estimation is based on consecutive measurements of short sequences of a probe state $\sqrt{\rho}\rho\sqrt{\rho}$. The second algorithm uses a different approach, related to the quantum Gibbs mechanism, measuring the entropy with a greater degree of accuracy, however at an increased cost, proportional to the number of principal components. Both algorithms show promising results for low and high phase error ratios. The entropy estimation is considered successful if the error remains below 10% of the maximum entropy in the system. The probing algorithms show a significant reduction in measurement count compared to previous studies, achieving a factor proportional to the logarithm of the number of principal components for low error rates and a factor of $\sqrt{n}$ for high error rates. The number of principal components can be seen as a form of quantum support size, defining the dimensionality of the low entropy manifold $\sqrt{\rho}$. The algorithms demonstrate stability under various forms of imperfection, including noisy state preparation, noisy measurements, noisy quantum memory storage and retrieval, and random state pollution with a small probability. The analysis allows us to study the interplay between quantum entropy and the principles of quantum measurement, illustrating how certain principles of integration in quantum mechanics are reinterpreted in the context of random matrix theory. The results suggest a potential link with recent breakthroughs in estimating entropy in classical systems. The study also investigates potential applications and implications of entropy estimation for quantum certification and quantum hacking techniques. The methods have been implemented in a publicly available Python code, attached to the arXiv document, tested with simulations involving up to 80 qubits. The entropy estimation reaches the theoretical bounds predicted by the quantum Cram\'{e}r-Rao theorem, showing proximity to the critical point of the quantum Gibbs mechanism. However, for low error rates, the algorithms tend to overestimate the entropy, indicating a tendency to conserve quantum information. The quantum entropy estimation presents a balance of resources, bounded by the quantum capacity of entanglement, which may have implications for the design of future quantum algorithms. The study also explores the universality of the results, examining entropy estimation for different forms of entropy, including the multiplicative R\'{e}nyi entropy and the logarithmic quantum entropy. Hospitals encode patient data in standardized formats to track medical conditions, treatments, and outcomes, utilizing coding systems such as the International Classification of Diseases (ICD). Human-coded data is often prone to errors due to medical complexity and coding ambiguities. Research aims to improve data quality through machine learning, specifically supervised learning, which relies on experts to correct mistakes and develop training datasets. To reduce the reliance on experts, this study employs semi-supervised learning using patient information to create a reliable training set. We analyzed hospital admissions data from the Ohio Patient Discharge Data Set to compare self-supervised and supervised learning approaches for ICD coding. Both methods were evaluated using standard classification metrics on the dataset's first 500 entries, with the top 10 frequent codes manually annotated for comparison. The results show that self-supervised learning outperforms supervised learning in multi-label classification tasks. To facilitate widespread adoption, we also developed a Python package to streamline the ICD coding process, making it easily accessible for replication and use in similar applications. This research is contingent on the assumption that nearby codes share similar characteristics, with potential extensions to other coding systems. To address the challenge of limited training data, this work explores self-supervised learning as an effective strategy for improving medical data quality. It is anticipated that the implemented approach will enhance the accuracy of ICD coding, a skill previously requiring extensive medical training. We strive to make our custom-built Python package, PythonICD, a useful tool for the community, allowing for easy replication of our methods and efficient encoding of new datasets. The conventional approach to traffic analysis relies on two distinct types of data: historical traffic data and detailed trip information. This double-sourced approach combines large datasets of origin-destination flows with simulated data based on real traffic patterns. However, the increasing availability of daily traffic data has led to a renewed focus on using such data exclusively, eliminating the need for trip records. This is made possible by the advancement in deep learning techniques that enable the direct estimation of origin-destination demands from canoptic data. Despite these developments, the exclusive use of canoptic data remains suboptimal due to the inherent limitations of traffic data, which often results in inaccurate predictions of high-frequency flows. This research aims to address this issue by applying statistical principles to canoptic data, leveraging the underlying structure of trip patterns to improve origin-destination demand estimation. This is achieved by treating the data as the outcome of repeated trips and applying statistical methods to model trip behavior. Our results indicate that incorporating knowledge of origin-destination patterns within the statistical model significantly enhances the accuracy of high-frequency flow estimation. Moreover, the canoptic data preprocessed through this statistical approach outperforms other canoptic-based methods, demonstrating the significance of addressing the limitations of traffic data through advanced statistical methods. Furthermore, our results suggest that the canoptic data preprocessed through this statistical approach is more compatible with trip records, emitting a reduced error when compared to simulated trip data. This is particularly valuable in contemporary traffic analysis, where the simulated trip data is increasingly used as a baseline for validating traffic models. Ultimately, our research offers a traffic modeling approach that optimizes the use of daily traffic data while incorporating knowledge of origin-destination patterns, leading to a more accurate estimation of high-frequency origin-destination demands. Moreover, our study has identified key insights into the structure of trip patterns, which can be applied in various traffic analysis applications beyond demand estimation. It is worth noting that our research is uniquely positioned to address these challenges, leveraging advanced deep learning techniques in conjunction with statistical methods to optimize the utilization of daily traffic data. By applying fundamental statistical principles to the complex data, our work provides a solid foundation for future developments in traffic modeling and analysis. Additionally, our results can be tailored to accommodate specific data formats and apply to diverse urban environments, making our approach highly adaptable and comprehensive. Lastly, our results are designed to be scalable, enabling the extraction and processing of data at an unprecedented large scale, thereby facilitating the practical implementation of our findings in real-world applications. This research will be presented at the 12th International Conference on Road Transportation

In an array of coupled oscillators with randomly connected interactions, our research reveals that diverse systems consisting of chaotic, conditional-chaotic, and orderly oscillating networks synchronize in the same uniform phase. However, our analysis focuses solely on the asymptotic, uniform-phase synchronized state, and not on the dynamics leading to this state. Furthermore, we found that weak internode connections are necessary for achieving such uniform-phase synchronization in large networks. Otherwise, leading nodes assume the role of 'conductors,' regulating the'music' emanating from the rest of the network. Our study uses numerical methods to analyze two types of oscillator arrays: those governed by Rössler equations, and those representing coupled chaotic Bird's stochastic differential equations. Our results indicate that weak internode connections correspond to a particular, delicate balance in the strength of individual interactions with the leading node. This finding underlines the fundamental distinction between 'orderly' and 'chaotic' dynamics in these oscillator arrays, and their implications for achieving uniform-phase synchronization. Additionally, we explored the relationship between synchronization and the topological structure of oscillator connections. Our research indicates that uniform-phase synchronization is predominantly observed in highly disconnected networks, whereas orderly or chaotic states prevail in densely interconnected networks. Conversely, we found that in highly disconnected networks, leading nodes typically exhibit orderly oscillating behavior, whereas uniform-phase synchronization is more common with chaotic leading nodes in densely interconnected networks. Lastly, our study also touched upon the phenomenon of'multiple attractors,' a characteristic feature of chaotic oscillator arrays, and its influence on uniform-phase synchronized states. Moreover, we discovered that the robustness of uniform-phase synchronized states varies greatly between different systems consisting of different oscillator arrays. This work presents a comprehensive music dataset named MusicTM-Dataset that enhances cross-modal retrieval capabilities by enabling the learning of unified representations for audio, image, and text components. The dataset is constructed from three distinct music datasets: the Million Song Dataset, Music21, and LyricWiki. Our resource comprises three modalities of data: musical scores with text, musical excerpts in WAV format, and song lyrics in Wikipedia format. The researchers' objective is to develop a system that can recognize music pieces based solely on visual scores or song lyrics. After converting existing datasets into a compatible format, our collection consists of 179,472 musical score-image-text triples and 21,310 audio-score-text triples. Notably, we also offer preprocessed musical scores in the Music21 XML format to facilitate the development of score-based recognition systems. Our research demonstrates the efficacy of various deep learning models in extracting robust features from each modality and achieving satisfactory results in the recognition tasks. In optical systems where the non-linear interaction depends on light intensity, research has demonstrated that dark solitons exhibit resistance to collapse under small changes in light intensity. To investigate this further, researchers have developed a generalized version of the Gross-Pitaevskii equation for describing dark solitons in 1D optical systems, taking into account variations in light intensity and non-linear interaction strength. By analyzing the equation, researchers found that the stability of dark solitons depends on the balance between counteracting effects of light variations and non-linear interaction, resulting in an exponential decrease in soliton lifetime with increasing light variations. To verify their findings, researchers have conducted numerical simulations of dark solitons in Kerr-type media with varying light sensitivity, observing the emergence of soliton instability in all cases. Notably, researchers found that the rate of soliton instability is sensitive to the phase of light waves, with rapid decay in coherent dark solitons and slower decay in anti-coherent dark solitons. To better understand the implications of their findings, researchers have developed a simplified mathematical model of soliton instability, revealing the underlying physical mechanisms responsible for soliton decay. Based on their research, scientists conclude that dark solitons are generally unstable under normal conditions but can become stable with sufficient light variations and non-linear interaction, opening up potential applications of dark solitons in optical communication and quantum computing. Additionally, researchers suggest that dark solitons could be used as stable carriers for the transmission of quasi-atomic solitons in optical systems with adjustable light interaction. With their research, scientists have greatly expanded their understanding of dark soliton stability, paving the way for future research into new dark soliton applications. Through a methodical evaluation strategy, we showcase Lotse's capabilities, starting with an in-depth analysis of state-of-the-art direction representations followed by a comparison with six prominent direction representation methods. Next, we conduct user studies to examine Lotse's practical applications, featuring 30 participants from the visual analytics community. Following this, we undertake a task-oriented evaluation of an implementation of Lotse within VaSys, a system for creating interactive visualizations, before finally showcasing the benefits of Lotse through a practical example use case. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that Lotse is a practical solution for direction representation that aligns with the needs and preferences of visual analytics developers. Furthermore, our comprehensive evaluation process serves as a guideline for effectively evaluating and comparing direction representation structures in the context of visual analytics. The proposed Lotse structure, as well as VaSys with integrated Lotse direction representation, are made available online for development and testing purposes. The problem of solving cardiac mechanics problems is examined. These problems, characterized by partial differential equations (PDEs) in three-dimensional space, often require large computational grids. For a wide range of parameters, explicit solution methods are impractical, making implicit solutions necessary. This necessitates the use of linear systems that need to be solved. Because the size of these systems can be enormous (several million unknowns), high-performance computational methods are essential. This study explores three approaches - Multi-Level Preconditioning, Hierarchical Matrices, and Graph Sparsification - to tackle this task. A comprehensive analysis is presented, covering code optimization, graph structure, performance, and outcome. Specifically, the focus is on the Flexible Multiscale Framework and the Modular Parameterization Technique for Cardiac Mechanics. These problems, characterized by low-frequency oscillations, require specialized treatment of low-frequency components in addition to implicit smoothing. Three distinct configurations are examined: the Graph Sparsification Approach, the Multi-Level Preconditioning Approach, and the Hierarchical Matrices Approach. While all three techniques yield comparable results, the Graph Sparsification Approach requires significantly fewer computations, although memory usage increases. A critical parameter is the level of decomposition in multi-level and hierarchical methods. Too few levels lead to inadequate sparse structures, while too many levels result in excessive computations and inadequate performance. Another crucial parameter is the graph size, particularly for Graph Sparsification, as it directly affects performance and numerical results. This study is a first to combine cardiac mechanics and linear system solvers with multi-level techniques and hierarchical methods. Despite the relatively slow monolithic approach, the Graph Sparsification Approach outperforms multi-level and hierarchical methods by a significant margin. This remarkable performance, coupled with the relatively low memory usage, makes the Graph Sparsification Approach an ideal candidate for complex cardiac mechanics problems. Furthermore, the code, although initially complex and difficult to understand, was extensively optimized to minimize memory usage and enhance performance. Key strategies, such as code splitting and temporary memory elimination, greatly enhanced overall efficiency and scalability. This work, characterized by comprehensive analysis and code optimization, lays the foundation for successful deployment in cardiac mechanics problems. In addition to the research findings, the study also shares knowledge with others through shared code repositories and benchmark problems. This study investigates the potential of accessible data sources to supply COVID-19 infection rates and related information in South Africa. A comparative evaluation of official infection rate data and three publicly available datasets was conducted. The analysis compared infection rates from the government-provided COVID-19 South Africa Public Dataset and two social media datasets with official infection rate statistics from the National Institute for Communicable Diseases. Our findings show that the social media datasets accurately predicted COVID-19 trends, including both increases and decreases in infections. Moreover, the social media datasets detected shifts in infection dynamics sooner than the government-provided dataset. Consequently, these sources could serve as supplementary tools for informing pandemic policy and strategy. Nevertheless, relying solely on social media data is not sufficient due to existing inaccuracies and seasonal flu-related flaws. To rectify this, combining social media data with other available sources, such as mobile device data, may yield more reliable pandemic prediction outcomes. Such hybrid approaches are thought to be particularly effective in countries with limited testing capacity. Ultimately, this research underscores the importance of utilizing non-traditional data sources to supplement the pandemic surveillance toolkit. My recommendations for the Pandemic Surveillance Consortium's methods and procedures are outlined below. Firstly, using social media data for infection rate forecasting shows promising signs. Therefore, this data should continue to be collected and analyzed. Secondly, we suggest that both government and industry parties collaborate to develop a unified data pipeline for infection rate forecasting. Thirdly, we recommend that the National Institute for Communicable Diseases serves as the central office for coordinating the response to the pandemic. Fourthly, we propose that the Institute utilize data from multiple sources, including social media and mobile devices, to inform the pandemic. Finally, we suggest that these diverse data sources be presented to the public through a single, unified interface. These recommendations may facilitate better decision-making at both the governmental and individual levels. In the end, we hope that this research will contribute to an accelerated response to the pandemic in South Africa. The social media data can be obtained at https://github.com/sa-covid19/sa-covid19-social-media. Mobile device data can be obtained at https://github.com/sa-covid19/sa-covid19-mobile. All codes and data have been shared publicly for the benefit of the pandemic community.

The Algebraic Branch Splitting (ABS) method provides a way to calculate polynomial roots by dividing polynomials based on known root values. It also allows generating rational parameterizations for trilinear forms that have known root counts. However, the chosen division is not unique and depends on additional algebraic constraints, which can be used to refine the method. Not all of these additional conditions are necessary to establish the uniqueness of root patterns, especially when working with specific root values as division points. Nonetheless, imposing these conditions facilitates the computation of unique root patterns. When these conditions are met, even highly complex forms can be solved easily, as demonstrated by our calculation of the H2 formula with the specified root values. Our analysis also shows that the H2 formula can be generalized to higher degree forms in a straightforward manner. Furthermore, the calculations of these forms are highly efficient and can be automated. As a result, the calculated root patterns are provided in closed form for degree 6 and 8 forms, as well as for degree 12 forms up to a certain threshold. Additionally, we have released a publicly available computation program that can calculate these root patterns for degree 12 and 14 forms, as well as confirm the root counts for degree 10 and 12 forms. As a result, the use of standard evaluation metrics is limited in this task. In this research, we introduce novel, refined assessment metrics that successfully differentiate between accurate and erroneous predictions. We examine the distinction between two forms of measurement influence, strong and feeble, within the context of quantum theory. In scenarios where a measurement outcome does not depend on the system's state, strong and feeble measurements exhibit equivalent effects on the system. However, strong measurements inevitably lead to mixed states, whereas feeble measurements can result in both mixed and pure states, depending on the system's initial condition. We derive conditions for feeble measurements to preserve pure states, and vice versa, and discuss the implications for quantum information processing. Furthermore, we discuss the maintenance of pure states in dimensions higher than two and the constraints such measurements impose on pure state sets within those dimensions. Lastly, we extend our analysis to the case of multiple subsystem measurements. Our research provides a framework for categorizing and comparing different types of measurement influence and their effects on quantum states. In particular, we identify a measurement cost associated with feeble measurements and establish a trade-off between measurement influence and this cost, which is expressed in terms of the logarithm of the minimal eigenvalue of the measurement operator. Our findings shed light on the fundamental characteristics of measurement influence and its implications for quantum state dynamics. In the standard RAM model, operations aside from reading or writing memory content are considered to take linear time. However, in a modified RAM model with constant-time addition, executing basic arithmetic operations like subtraction, multiplication, and division should take constant time as well. We identify the specific sequences of addition operations needed to achieve this. Specifically, we demonstrate that any sequence of addition can be performed in constant time if we allow for a fixed number of indirect memory accesses, denoted as k, and if the maximum value stored in memory does not exceed 2^N, where N represents the number of bits in memory addresses. This insight leads us to formulate a fundamental question: can non-fixed constant values be efficiently stored in memory with a fixed number of addresses? Our findings reveal that if memory locations contain distinct values, they cannot be used to store the result of a division operation. Our results demonstrate the stability of the RAM model with constant-time addition and show that the time complexity of algorithms executed on this model is unaffected by the number of memory locations. We resolve this stability issue by finding the specific sequences of addition operations needed to achieve it. Our work is documented in the paper titled "Which computational operations can be executed in constant time in the RAM model with addition?".

This approach utilizes two-photon absorption within a highly resistive material to monitor transient electric currents as a means of discovering spatial variations in charge transport properties. Our technique was utilized to investigate a synthetic single-crystalline diamond in both [100] and [111] orientations. Our results show that under two-photon absorption at 800 nm, we observe significant charge transfer in the [100] orientation, but little to no charge transfer in the [111] orientation. Additionally, we slice the [100] sample in half and expose the surfaces to radiation, leading to the accumulation of charge at the interface. Our findings reveal a substantial boost in charge transfer when one surface is treated. Our work showcases the capability of the two-photon absorption boundary transient-current method to inspect three-dimensional charge transport in solid materials by detecting transient electric currents produced by two-photon absorption. Pulsar wind nebulae are thought to originate from the Friedmann-Robertson-Walker expansion of electron--positron clouds emitted by dying pulsars. We investigate the gamma-ray emission of these objects using a detailed model that takes into account particle injection and absorption processes. By applying this to a sample of 27 gamma-ray pulsar wind nebulae, we can fit their gamma-ray spectra. However, our simulation struggles to replicate the observed gamma-ray photon counts for many of these objects. This could indicate additional particle injection from stellar winds or other factors, or the presence of non-radiative mechanisms such as magnetic-field-instability-powered emission. We also observe a discrepancy between our calculated pulsar birth velocities and those predicted by simulation, suggesting that a significant number of pulsars must be hidden either behind the Galaxy's central ridge or within dense molecular clouds. By analyzing the gamma-ray luminosity of these wind nebulae, we conclude that the majority of Galactic TeV pulsar wind nebulae remain undiscovered. Our estimates of pulsar spin-down energy and W3C295 pulsar wind nebulae's underlying pulsar luminosity align with each other and show a broad correlation with the pulsar's spin-down rate. This relationship holds significant implications for future studies of these objects, as it allows us to extend our analysis to a larger sample of wind nebulae, including those without gamma-ray coverage. Utilizing our confirmed model, we estimate the number of undiscovered TeV wind nebulae in the Galaxy, which is dominated by the Galaxy's central region and areas obscured by molecular clouds. Finally, based on our prediction of pulsar wind nebulae's spatial distribution, we suggest several locations for future study with the Gamma-ray Laboratory for Astronomical Studies. We introduce a weather classification dataset comprising 192,000 images, organized into 10 distinct weather conditions and 5 intensity levels. To mitigate the challenges of limited dataset performance, we develop an enhanced training methodology involving image augmentation. Evaluating various Convolutional Neural Network architectures on our dataset, we observe that PreAct ResNet-18 delivers the most satisfactory results, achieving a multi-class accuracy of 93% across all weather conditions. Notably, our dataset and corresponding training methodology demonstrate effective outcomes, even with models trained on just 10,000 images. The proposed dataset and associated training techniques are intended to support the development of intelligent vehicles capable of recognizing and adapting to diverse weather scenarios. The dataset, source code, and research results are publicly available for research purposes.

Our research focuses on developing an automated system for identifying and classifying ten distinct weather types from ten categories, including clear skies, overcast skies, rain, snow, snow-grit, snow-ice, fog, fog-mist, haze, and haze-mist, from images captured by vehicle-mounted cameras. To train this system, we have assembled a large-scale dataset comprising 192,000 images, organized into five intensity levels for each weather type. However, our initial experiments revealed that traditional deep learning models produce subpar results on this dataset. To address this challenge, we have developed an innovative training approach, image augmentation, to enhance the performance of our system. Specifically, we employ data augmentation and utilize a small dataset for training, resulting in a 7% improvement in accuracy from 85.5% to 92.5%. Furthermore, we evaluate various Convolutional Neural Network architectures on our dataset, achieving a multi-class accuracy of 93% with PreAct ResNet-18. Notably, our research demonstrates that models trained on a small dataset of 10,000 images can still achieve an accuracy of 87.5%, encompassing a wide range of weather conditions. To the best of our knowledge, our research presents the first systematic evaluation of deep learning models for classifying ten distinct weather types from ten categories. Additionally, our dataset and associated training approaches can be applied to other scenarios, such as intelligent vehicles, where adaptive systems are required to navigate various weather conditions. The proposed dataset and training methodologies are intended to facilitate research in these areas.

Recent advancements in research have uncovered significant opportunities for Deep Reinforcement Learning to overcome challenges in Natural Language Processing. Despite this, numerous hurdles remain in employing DRL effectively to produce authentic language descriptions. Multiple factors contribute to this complexity, including the ambiguity of words, inconsistencies in data, and the diversity of possible descriptions. To date, few studies have analyzed the fundamentals of DRL in NLP, leaving a substantial knowledge gap. This review aims to bridge this disparity by exploring existing studies and outlining the necessary fundamentals, while also identifying prevalent empirical methods and proposed solutions to achieve better performance. To this end, we examine the applications of DRL in NLP, focusing on its practical applications and the underlying theoretical principles. We also discuss the potential pitfalls and future directions for researchers, in addition to highlighting the recent breakthroughs and potential avenues for further investigation. By providing an in-depth overview of the subject, we hope to inspire novel approaches to DRL in NLP. The source code for this review can be accessed at https://github.com/bcmi/AugSL.

Recent advancements in large language models have led to superior performance in open-domain conversation tasks. However, current models often mix role definitions within their text inputs, limiting their ability to construct a more controlled and structured conversation system. To address this, we utilize role definitions separately as class labels and design a novel dataset processing method to fine-tune LLMs for our needs. We also introduce a new dataset called "The Role of Technology in Daily Life" (RTDD) comprising 185 discussions with clear role definitions. Our research demonstrates the potential of fine-tuning LLMs with a well-curated dataset like RTDD to create a role-defined open-domain conversation system. Such an approach has vast potential for applications in fields like customer service, technical support, and sales. With continued development and enhancement of both LLMs and related training datasets, we can build a more sophisticated conversation system to guide individuals in understanding the daily roles technology can play. The code and RTDD dataset for this project are available on GitHub at <https://github.com/jayantasharma/Role Defined Conversation >. rtdd.github.io was also created to showcase the dataset and code. A reliable and efficient communication system known as the signaling game is proposed, which combines a neural-based inference mechanism with a semantic framework. To achieve optimal performance, novel strategies for channel input and detection have been developed. By applying deep learning techniques to the cognitive radio, complex signals are interpreted into meaningful symbols, leading to enhanced semantic transmission efficiency. Experimental results indicate that the proposed system outperforms conventional methods in semantic error rate and also attains a higher information transfer rate than frequency hopping multiple access. This new system offers a promising approach to emerging semantic communications technologies. A detailed explanation of the underlying signaling game is provided through a mathematical analysis that includes an optimal Nash equilibrium solution. Furthermore, a novel neural network architecture, the causal memory network, is designed to address the limitations of current sequence-to-sequence models, which often rely on pre-defined causal relationships, by learning to establish such connections itself. When tested on the proposed signaling game, the causal memory network demonstrated superior performance compared to existing models, such as the transformer network. A corresponding reduction in semantic error rate was observed without compromising information transfer rate. This research lays a foundational understanding of the emerging semantic communication technology and provides insightful quantitative analysis to guide its development. A comparative study of semantic error rate and information transfer rate is also provided to facilitate the design of semantic communication systems. Additionally, the study explores the feasibility of using deep learning techniques to expand the semantic communication vocabulary and discovered that using sequential RNN models can generate words more efficiently than other models, leading to enhanced semantic error rate performance. In the data mining and machine learning communities, predictive modeling has long been the primary focus, with applications ranging from medical diagnosis to online recommendations and text analysis. This study shifts away from traditional predictive models, instead focusing on term prediction in texts to uncover hidden patterns. Naive Bayes is adapted for this task by converting its classification capability into a probabilistic generator, producing unexpected terms as a natural byproduct. To further uncover latent patterns, two additional models, one based on co-occurrence and latent binary vectors, and another built around document similarity, are developed and demonstrated to outperform Naive Bayes in a predictive framework. The proposed approach is evaluated using statistical tests and real-world datasets, showcasing its ability to reveal human-intuitive patterns, such as geographic and temporal terms, when combined with pre-existing knowledge. Furthermore, two application examples are showcased to highlight the potential uses of this approach, revealing its capability to reveal latent patterns in medical texts and book summaries. Lastly, two possible future extensions of this work are suggested, involving the enhancement of its performance through the incorporation of external knowledge and the exploration of its compatibility with deep learning methods. The research code is publicly available on GitHub. The research findings suggest that Naive Bayes, adapted for term prediction, can uncover latent patterns in texts, revealing performance improvements over models built around document similarity and latent patterns. Additionally, the study demonstrates the capability of these models to reveal latent patterns in medical texts and book summaries, while also outlining potential future extensions of these models.
