Presence-absence data is represented as binary vectors or matrices consisting of zeros and ones, typically denoting the presence of something in a specific location. These data types are commonly found across disciplines such as ecology, chemistry, and linguistics. Researchers often utilize multivariate data analysis techniques to explore the structure and similarity within such data by converting eachties into numerical values or applying clustering methods directly to the binary format. Our study compares the efficiency of different clustering methods for high-dimensional presence-absence data based on several criteria including computational speed, typological similarity, and solution stability. Our results indicate that many clustering algorithms exhibit comparable performance in terms of speed, but their effectiveness varies significantly according to the metric used to evaluate typological similarity. However, when we focus on solution stability, our findings suggest that methods which treat absence as information and analyze the data in a binary format generally outperform their counterparts. Additionally, our study reveals that many clustering methods share common characteristics, and our analysis highlights the potential pitfalls of certain clustering practices. Ultimately, our research aims to contribute to an informed discussion on the appropriate use of clustering methods in the context of presence-absence data. Our study's openness extends to data, methods, and software used throughout the study. In recent years, salient object detection using deep learning techniques has received significant attention, but dealing with objects of various sizes remains a significant challenge. To address this issue, our proposed framework combines a globally informed feature extraction module and a locally sensitive refinement module to improve salient object detection across different object scales. Utilizing a self-encoders mechanism, the feature extraction module integrates global context and context-sensitivity to extract relevant features, followed by a refinement module that utilizes a conditional attention mechanism and a correlation filter to improve salient object detection. Extensive experiments on various datasets demonstrate the excellence of our proposed framework, with our method outperforming state-of-the-art approaches on six benchmark datasets. Furthermore, our method's effectiveness is showcased through rigorous ablation studies and qualitative analysis. Our proposed framework is particularly effective for salient object detection in scenarios with diverse object scales. With the integration of global and local information, our method achieves remarkable performance on benchmark datasets, showcasing its versatility and effectiveness. The source code of our framework is available at https://github.com/Chen-123456/UE-SOD. Social media is a significant source of information for modern society, with vast amounts of data being generated daily. Despite its benefits, social media also poses significant problems, including the spread of aggressive tweets. In an effort to address this issue, Twitter launched a classification system for such posts, labeling them as abusive or offensive. In response to a call for participation in SemEval 2019-2020, we developed two systems, one basic and one advanced, designed to classify aggressive tweets. The basic system relied on support vector machines (SVMs) and word embeddings from three different data sets, including train, test, and validation data. In contrast, our advanced system built upon the basic one, incorporating additional advanced features, pre-trained models, and a voting mechanism. Ultimately, our submissions met the deadline, with our entries earning top spots in two categories for category prediction and binary classification. Our research is a stepping stone for studying social media toxicity, with room for growth and improvement. Going forward, we intend to refine our approach, incorporating more cutting-edge techniques, particularly in deep learning and natural language processing (NLP). Additionally, we will utilize umlating models with similar objectives to understand and address problems like aggressive tweets better. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and significant variability in handwriting styles across different regions. To overcome this problem, we focus on developing a method that generates large amounts of high-quality synthetic data from a limited number of perfect transcripts and corresponding image segments. Since CDHTR requires taking both text and image into account during training, we propose using a normalizing transformation to eliminate the influence of text content and instead leverage image features and a pre-existing text dataset to create synthetic data. To validate our approach, we conducted experiments on three handwritten languages and compared its effectiveness against two alternative methods one of which involves generating random characters. While the results indicate that our approach outperforms the others, we observed that the success of this strategy heavily depends on the quality of the used image features. To address this issue, we further developed a supplementary strategy called Single-shot Compositional Data Creation (SSCDC) which utilizes a fully convolutional auto-encoder to create synthetic data from single instances of handwritten characters, thereby producing more realistic results. Through a series of ablation studies, we analyzed SSDC's potential to improve models trained on HTR datasets. The source code for our approach is available at https://github.com/asharaki/HTR_Composition.

Furthermore, our approach allows us to extend the composition mapping theorem from the upper half-plane to the upper half-plane with a Lipschitz boundary, which in turn generalizes the theorem to the Bergman spaces of simply connected, strictly convex domains. Up to 4-loop order, the dual-loop method correctly reproduces the point limit of the scattering amplitude, thereby validating the method. High-performance computing on field-programmable gate arrays exploits the parallelism inherent in signal processing, but achieving parallelism in object-oriented programming is more challenging, primarily due to memory allocation issues. To address this problem, we developed DynaSOAr, a concurrent memory allocator for use on multicore central processing units and graphics processing units. This allocator optimizes memory on the host CPU, allowing for efficient memory usage on the GPU through a dynamic allocation strategy. Since dynamic memory allocation on GPUs is restricted, DynaSOAr also provides manual memory management options. We tested DynaSOAr in a real-world application, specifically in finite element method calculations, and found that our allocator outperforms existing solutions by up to 30% on CPU and by up to 25% on GPU. Furthermore, when compared to static memory allocation, DynaSOAr showed a 10% time reduction and a 25% energy consumption savings. We also found that our allocator can reduce energy consumption by removing unused GPU memory, resulting in a 10% to 25% decrease in energy consumption after compilation. To facilitate easy adoption into existing GPU-based object-oriented development, we provided a detailed tutorial on integrating DynaSOAr into numerical field simulations. This tutorial, combined with the source code and technical details, will be made available for public use upon publication. In addition to outperforming current memory allocation strategies, DynaSOAr is also compatible with multiple programming languages, such as Fortran, C++, and Python, making it a versatile tool for various GPU-based object-oriented development tasks. We identified two key areas for further improvement, including concurrent allocation for particle-based applications and the use of hardware-determined memory allocation, which we plan to address in future research. These potential areas for improvement were also discussed in detail. To summarize, DynaSOAr is a novel allocator that offers several benefits over existing solutions, primarily due to its ability to efficiently manage memory through a dynamic strategy, while also providing manual memory management options and supporting multiple programming languages. We tested and validated DynaSOAr in real-world applications and found that it significantly outperforms current allocators, as well as reduces energy consumption by optimizing GPU memory usage. This rate-based model accounts for non-linear electron dynamics among different orbital states, transport processes, and phonon effects to capture the slow time-scale changes, and it aligns with density functional theory calculations for time scales up to hundreds of femtoseconds. A construction for (4/3)-spanners involves selecting edges from the Euclidean nearest neighbor graph. This research presents a new technique for creating word alignments in bilingual documents. Unlike traditional methods, this approach doesn't need extensive, specially formatted training data and can produce accurate alignments at the word level. Even with minimal native language skills, it adapts to a new language pair by drawing from publicly accessible bilingual sources, such as Wikipedia. This capability makes it useful for various tasks and can be further refined with additional knowledge to improve its overall efficiency and accuracy.

Word alignment is a fundamental task in NLP and is used to enhance various models and applications including machine translation, domain-adaptation, and text manipulation. Typically, alignment is done on large, parallel corpora but transferring these alignments to new, unrelated texts can be challenging. This research aims to overcome these limitations by directly creating word alignments in bilingual sentences regardless of their origin.

There are two primary approaches to word alignment: statistical methods and supervised learning. Statistical models, such as those based on IBM models, are straightforward to apply but their accuracy is generally limited. Supervised learning, on the other, requires extensive, high-quality training data which can be costly and time-consuming to obtain.

This research presents a new technique for word alignment using bilingual data from external sources. This approach is based on analyzing sentence pairs and comparing their similarities to build word alignments. Since it uses bilingual data from external sources, it is not necessary to format large, parallel corpora or ensure data quality.

In our experiments, we used Wikipedia's bilingual pages as our source of bilingual data. We developed an algorithm to analyze Wikipedia's interlings and established a connection between words that share similar meanings across different languages. When confronted with a new, unrelated text, this algorithm uses Wikipedia's bilingual data to build word alignments in real-time.

Our results show that using Wikipedia's bilingual data alone, we can achieve accuracy rates of 57.5% for alignment coverage (i.e., the percentage of words in source sentences that have an alignment) and 66.3% for alignment precision (i.e., the percentage of accurately aligned words in source sentences) without any further training or data.

To improve our model's efficiency and accuracy, we used Wikipedia's bilingual data to create clusters of similar words in each language. We then analyzed these clusters to build word alignments and compared our approach with state-of-the-art algorithms using real-world datasets.

Our results show that using Wikipedia's bilingual data and clustering technique, we can achieve accuracy rates of 58.6% for alignment coverage and 67.4% for alignment precision.

We introduce a distorted resolvent method to build Nash equilibria for a wide range of econometric models, encompassing single and multi-product industries, as well as transport costs. This novel approach deforms the resolvent operator to facilitate analytical and numerical solutions. Both analytical and numerical examples are provided to illustrate the method's effectiveness, revealing its advantages in terms of computational efficiency and ease of implementation. Additionally, we examine the distoration of operators and their implications for Nash equilibrium construction. Our findings indicate that distoration can enhance computational convergence and even permit the construction of Nash equilibria in models previously intractable with standard methods. Like many operator distortions, the resolvent distortion we propose has a straightforward economic interpretation, reflecting adjustments made to firms' marginal costs to ensure the existence of a Nash equilibrium. In this spirit, we explore a broader class of resolvent distorsions, encompassing both our previous example and an alternative scenario where firms' price adjustments are distorted. Both of these alternative distorsions can be applied to models of competitive equilibrium. Our analysis provides a unified framework for understanding the role of distorsions in Nash equilibrium and competitive equilibrium models. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the distorted resolvent method offers a versatile tool for tackling a diverse array of economic equilibrium problems. We examined a two-dimensional system where rigid triangular sectors interact with each other. This system was realized using particles with fixed splay angles, which formed stages with inherent symmetries. These stages were characterized by the absence of any sliding or twisting motion. We found that as we decreased particle size, the number of configurations in each stage decreased, thereby determining the order in which these stages occur. Additionally, we computed the entropy changes associated with these stages and found that these changes remain constant when expressed in terms of the surface tension for systems composed of benzene molecules. This observation suggests that the stages represent distinct configurations relevant to the understanding of two-dimensional systems composed of rigid triangular sectors. Furthermore, we explored the stages in systems lacking symmetry, which were generated using particles with randomly assigned splay angles. In these cases, the number of configurations in each stage increases with particle size, thereby determining the sequence in which these stages occur. We found that these stages comprise multiple configurations and that certain stages exhibit high occupational entropy. Additionally, we computed the thermal changes associated with these stages and observed that these changes vary as a function of the angle distribution of particle splay. This angle distribution affects the sequence in which these stages occur, thereby influencing the thermal stability of these configurations. Based on these findings, we conclude that the stages in systems lacking symmetry are influenced by the inherent structural properties of these particles, thereby demanding a more complex determination of these stages. Moreover, we observed that the stages in two-dimensional systems, whether symmetric or not, can be effectively probed using scanning tunneling microscopy. This technique enables us to explore these stages at constant temperature and to determine their sequence in the limit of very small particle sizes. In the future, we aim to explore systems where particles undergo sliding or twisting motion and to investigate the stages in three-dimensional systems composed of rigid triangular sectors. Furthermore, we intend to compute the thermal changes associated with these stages in such systems and to extend our findings to understanding the structural properties of certain two-dimensional materials. In doing so, we hope to shed light on the essential physical phenomena governing these stages. In addition, we analyzed a system consisting of rigid triangular sectors with fixed splay angles, which exhibits stages characterized by the absence of any sliding or twisting motion. We found that as particle size decreases, the number of configurations in each stage decreases, thereby determining the sequence in which these stages occur. In particular, we explored two types of stages: those exhibiting high occupational entropy in systems lacking symmetry, as well as those exhibiting some occupational entropy in systems possessing symmetry.

In our research, we develop a novel modeling approach - known as the recursive field - that enables us to take advantage of efficient one-step recurrences. We examine the behavior of nanoscale objects falling through layers of granular material with a nonlinear spring constant, as well as a simplified model of feebly nonlinear arrays composed of identical masses and varying spring constants. In both cases, we find that localized energetic structures, or nanoptera, can form when an object falls through the layer and triggers a series of normal mode excitations that become locked in phase. In the nonlinear system, nanoptera move in discrete, predictable increments, while in the feebly nonlinear system, they move in continuous, gradual increments. In both cases, nanoptera exhibit permanent localization, with their motion unlikely to be dissipated by the surrounding layer. Additionally, we observe that when nanoptera move through the layer, they can become "trapped" at specific depths, as well as exhibit permanent localization. In the feebly nonlinear system, we identify multiple nanoptera modes and find that their motions are closely related to the dynamics of localized excitations observed in other granular systems. Finally, we speculate that nanoptera may also be observed in other types of granular systems.

Property-based learning in computer vision has seen success with convolutional neural networks but exploring other architectures is crucial for broadened applications and understanding. Vision Transformers (ViTs) naturally allow for property-aware learning due to their distinctive attention mechanisms, compared to traditional network designs. However, ViTs were initially primarily used for image classification, which doesn't leverage property information. To fully utilize ViT's potential, we investigate property-based learning within the framework, focusing on developing desirable properties for semantic segmentation. We show that by incorporating an auxiliary loss with linearly connected neurons, ViT can learn desirable properties for segmentation, similar to conventional ViT. The resulting model exhibits improved performance when compared to regular ViT and SegFormer, a leading segmentation model. Moreover, our property-based ViT demonstrates consistent and stable results across diverse datasets and domains, outperforming other methods in 9 out of 10 scenarios. The associated code and model will be publicly available.

We present a straightforward proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has a critical issue in terms of stability, specifically when using Sobolev spaces and certain types of Lorentz spaces, thereby confirming an earlier study by Bourgain and Li. The main idea of the proof involves creating a particular smooth and short-duration solution with significantly higher energy levels than a given initial input, which is tailored to exploit the limitations of certain assumptions on the nonlinear term's behavior as a operator. This approach enables us to bypass intricate analysis of the equations' Hamiltonian formulation and instead focus on basic properties of the equations, thereby making the proof much more accessible. Furthermore, this proof can be modified to apply to other types of equations, such as the Landau equations and the compressible Euler equations, within the same type of spaces. In addition, we've discovered a similar problem with the same types of equations in two-dimensional space, which we hope will serve as a useful test case to verify the correctness of numerical methods. Lastly, we've confirmed that the issue of stability is also present in several types of flows that are invariant, including those with periodic and pseudo-periodic characteristics. In particular, this applies to the torus and a specific case of pseudo-periodic flow that we've developed, which can serve as a useful test case to verify the correctness of numerical methods for these types of flows.

This project investigates the application of Bayesian neural networks in image concealment, focusing on reversing object masking. We develop a novel BNN-based technique, BNN-Reveal, to efficiently capture the uncertainty surrounding the hidden object's shape and position within a masked image. In contrast, conventional maximization-based approaches, such as NLM and LNP, are prone to over-smoothing due to their lack of uncertainty handling. Moreover, high computational requirements hinder their real-world usability. To address these limitations, we introduce BNN-Reveal, which can be trained with approximate EM iterations without compromising image quality. Our findings demonstrate that this method produces superior reconstruction results, with reduced computational and memory demands. Consequently, BNN-Reveal emerges as a viable and efficient solution for practical image concealment applications. Source code for this work is available at https://github.com/jayacma/BNN-Reveal. Experimental results and training examples can be found at https://rst.gs.nyu.edu/BNN-Reveal. BNN-Reveal has been patented under utility patent number 20210214142.

Secondly, the overall positive correlation in global solar faculae and bright points is predominantly driven by high-hentropy cases with strong horizontal magnetic fields that predominate at solar faculae and bright points, as these regions exhibit a strong inclination of magnetic fields towards the solar surface. This phenomenon causes an average positive correlation of solar faculae and bright points, as observed. We further speculate that our findings might extend to the solar cycle and other stars. In neurons, effective substance transport between a cell's body and distant synapses is crucial for communication between these critical components of the central nervous system. To maintain balance, neurons regulate substance transport via specialized mechanisms located at the transport sites. When these sites become congested due to the buildup of substances, it disrupts transport processes, leading to cellular dysfunction and ultimately, neurological disorders. For optimal substance transport, a balanced rate is necessary, thereby motivating the development of an optimization model that incorporates partial differential equations to simulate this process. This model utilizes a finite element method to discretize the equations and implements various transport mechanisms, such as active and passive transport, along with congestion regulation through feedback mechanisms like substance-dependent inhibition. To test the model's capabilities, scenarios involving different transport mechanisms and combinations of transport modes are analyzed, followed by an exploration of the effects of altered parameter values on substance distributions. Ultimately, this model provides a framework for understanding the intricate regulation of substance transport in neurons and identifying the underlying mechanisms contributing to cellular dysfunction and disease. Furthermore, this model can be adapted to investigate the regulation of substance transport in other cell types that utilize actin-based transport mechanisms. By incorporating user-friendly Graphical User Interface, this model enables researchers to easily modify and simulate various cellular conditions, thereby facilitating in-depth analysis and exploration of the underlying biology. In recent years, deep learning techniques have achieved remarkable success in video analysis.
This has led to the development of various video-based applications, with three-dimensional human body gesture recognition now becoming increasingly important.
Unfortunately, there is a lack of comprehensive benchmark datasets that measure state-of-the-art method performance in this field.
To address this issue, we present HUMBI, a massive collection of 3DCN challenges, comprising over 1.7 million multiview images and 180,000 video sequences.
This resource includes 40,000 training samples, 10,000 validation samples, and 20,000 test samples, all carefully crafted to evaluate 3DCN effectiveness from multiple viewpoints.
Our study compares the performance of conventional video models against state-of-the-art 3D point cloud models, highlighting the advantages of 3D point cloud models in predicting gesture accuracy.
Additionally, we propose an evaluation metric to gauge pose similarity between predicted and groundtruth human body gestures.
This allows us to establish a benchmark challenge, ranking current methods and leaving room for future improvement. HUMBI and related code and models are available at https://github.com/SamerRoussin/HUMBI. HUMBI.

A recent video super-resolution approach, BasicVSR, achieved notable success in improving video reconstruction quality through local re-generation and alignment. In an effort to further refine this technique, we conducted an in-depth analysis of BasicVSR and have developed a refined version, referred to as BasicVSR++. Our analysis of the method reveals that the key to its effectiveness lies in its alignment procedure, which generates inconsistent and incomplete frame values, ultimately hindering the overall performance of the network. To address this issue, we introduce two innovative methods, 2D/1D De-propagation and Multi-Gaussian Alignment, aimed at enhancing both the generation and alignment processes of the method. Through comprehensive evaluations conducted on diverse datasets, including Vid4, Rendered, and DPED, we observed a notable improvement in PSNR and SSIM scores of BasicVSR++ over the original BasicVSR, averaging 0.38/0.63 points, while also outperforming other state-of-the-art SR methods by 1/1.5 points. Our ultimate goal is to contribute to the development of more advanced video super-resolution approaches. BasicVSR++ code is available at https://github.com/OnionJuice/BasicVSR++.pdf. In multi-task reinforcement learning, related tasks often benefit from shared knowledge, but learning across multiple unconnected tasks can be wasteful and hindering.  We found that through evolutionary processes, modular structures emerge to avoid negative interactions between separate task learning modules.  By simulating a basic multi-task reinforcement learning scenario, we observed the emergence of coherent and useful policies, separate and distinct within individual learning modules.  As these modules interact with one another, they avoid overlapping policies from interfering with each other's learning.  This self-organizing process leads to improved overall policy performance overall.  Additionally, we found that these policies consist of separate modules each optimized for specific tasks, resulting in improved outcomes when applied together in combination.  This study provides the first evidence of the benefits of partitioning ideas in reinforcement learning settings.  Furthermore, we propose an approach to automatically discover these separation points, showing its potential to improve performance when applied to a complex multi-task reinforcement learning challenge. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of inherent pitch awareness in WN's architecture limits its application in generating raw pitch timbre signals. To overcome this, our proposed QPNet integrates WN with a pitch-sensitive dilated convolution network that adapts to various frequencies. Experimental results confirm that QPNet outperforms WN by generating higher quality audio samples at comparable rates. Additionally, QPNet demonstrates effective pitch control and sensitivity through parameter analysis. To the best of our knowledge, QPNet exhibits the largest range of pitch factors among existing deep generative models. Recommender systems' collaborative filtering method has seen advancements through the use of cooperative filtering (CF). CF's effectiveness relies on the idea that similar users share similar preferences. This preference similarity is utilized to estimate unknown ratings by analyzing the shared patterns among users' preferences. Biclustering, a data analysis technique, decomposes user-item matrices into sub-matrices representing shared preferences among groups of users and items. This research builds upon CF by incorporating the principles of biclustering. A novel CF approach called User-Specific Bicluster-based CF (USBCF) is presented, which focuses on addressing the issues of preference sparsity, subjectivity, and localization within the context of CF. USBCF is evaluated using real-world datasets and compared to existing CF methods. Evaluation results demonstrate that USBCF surpasses baseline CF approaches in predictive accuracy. Furthermore, USBCF's efficiency and scalability are evident in its ability to outperform CF models that rely on comprehensive training datasets. USBCF's capabilities can be accessed via an open-source implementation on GitHub. This study's contributions can be integrated into the development of recommender systems through the use of USBCF's source code. Research findings also offer insights for practitioners on the utilization of USBCF in real-world recommender system applications. Additionally, the source code may be utilized to repeat the study's results, which are comprised of 10 experimental variants of USBCF. These variants, along with the study's data preparation procedures, are detailed in the study's reproducibility script. USBCF's approaches can be applied across diverse CF models and datasets. This research presents three new avenues for future research alongside the source code. These avenues pertain to the exploration of the effects of varying bicluster sizes, the integration of external knowledge into CF through biclustering, and the utilization of deep learning methods that utilize shared user preferences. These research directions, along with the study's source code, can be accessed on GitHub. We introduce a solution to apply image styling techniques in a universal manner, enabling any two input images to be transformed into desired styles by forward and reverse tone mapping. The majority of existing approaches learn forward and reverse mapping models separately, in contrast to our style extraction algorithm that utilizes a single universal model for both tasks. To achieve this, we develop an innovative loss function that combines a permutation cycle loss and a cross-reconstruction loss to train the model. The style of any two image pairs can be learned and applied by simply optimizing our loss function, without the need for extensive data labeling. We showcase our method's effectiveness by applying it to multiple scenarios, such as achieving HDR from low-dynamic-range images, creating artistic effects, and transforming images to simulate real-world lighting scenarios. The proposed method demonstrates comparable or superior results to state-of-the-art baselines in various applications. The implementation will be made available on our website.

Identifying incidents on a dynamic network is essential for traffic management systems, allowing officials to adjust signal times to minimize congestion and reduce the impact of incidents on traffic flow. Traditional methods of incident detection by analyzing link-level data are insufficient for modern intelligent transportation systems, which operate on a larger scale. As such, there is a need for more advanced incident detection techniques. This work develops a novel approach for identifying incidents on a network by analyzing changes in traffic patterns. Traffic patterns are represented as graphs, where nodes with similar traffic flow rates are grouped together, and their connections are weighted by the similarity of these flow rates. When anomalies occur in a section of the network, it is indicated by a disruption in the pattern's structure, which can then be analyzed to determine the incident's location and extent. This approach is further modified to accommodate incident validation, allowing officials to adjust signal times and minimize congestion. Our method is now tested on a real-world network and compared to traditional incident detection methods, which are based on link-level data, to determine its effectiveness. Our results show that our approach is superior to traditional methods, particularly in identifying incidents on a partial section of the network. Daany is an open-source, cross-platform C# library focused on data analytics and linear algebra. This guide serves as a comprehensive developer manual, outlining Daany's features, functionality, and usage, as well as a listing of related papers. I argue that scientists like Galileo, who sought to apply mathematical methods to the study of physical phenomena, were actually representatives of a pre-existing mathematical tradition.  In contrast, philosophers like Kepler, who combined mathematics with speculative theories, represented a novel and influential ideological current.  A thorough examination of the works of Bonomopagni, Cataldi, and Galileo reveals that they drew upon ancient mathematical principles, whereas Kepler's opus magnum, Astronomia Nova, was notable for its integration of mathematics and philosophical discourse.  Kepler's innovative approach, which balanced skepticism with speculative philosophy, can be seen as a culmination of philosophical currents in the Scientific Revolution.  In contrast, Galileo's rejection of traditional authority and his emphasis on experimentation were more akin to the cultural transformations of the Enlightenment.  Ultimately, this paper strives to recast the narrative of the Scientific Revolution, one that celebrates the diverse influences of mathematics and philosophy that flourished during that time.  In doing so, it seeks to recover the lost voices of mathematicians and philosophers, allowing for a fresh appreciation of their significant contributions to the period. Our research aims to clarify these unique phenomena and their implications for the universe's early development. Importantly, these outcomes highlight the significance of non-Gaussian effects in understanding the primitive universe's profound phase transitions. Although these effects fade rapidly as equilibrium is achieved, their impact on early cosmological history deserves further investigation. We present a novel technique for machine-assisted documentation by leveraging a machine learning model to create concise, clear, and accurate summary comments for individual lines and groups of code. Our approach employs a data-driven approach to train a natural language generator on prevalent comment styles found in a large corpus of open-source software. By integrating the machine learning model into the code editing process, we enable developers to work alongside a'scribe' who provides expert summary comments, ultimately facilitating better program understanding, comprehension, and maintenance. Machine-assisted documentation has far-reaching implications: experiments demonstrate that the output comments are preferred over blank comments by human evaluators; the machine learning model can learn to provide comments that align with a programmer's experience level; and the process can be trained to conform to specific documentation guidelines. Ultimately, this technique provides a useful example of the beneficial outcomes that can be achieved through machine-assisted software development.
